meta.scope: Yangon-centred history of Myanmar / Burmese hip-hop: artists, crews, releases, songs, events, venues, topics, sources and typed relationships.

provenance.model: Every claim carries at least one source id. `status` on relationships is one of VERIFIED (human-checked), AI_EXTRACTED (pending review), CONFLICTED, REJECTED. `confidence` is high | medium | low.
provenance.copyright: Factual metadata only (names, dates, places). No article text, lyrics or images are redistributed. Copyrighted sources are cited for facts only.
provenance.caveat: Entities marked confidence low or status AI_EXTRACTED have not been human-verified. Render these with a visible "unverified" affordance.

guide.purpose: Single-file JSON for LLM consumption and UI generation. All cross-references are already resolved: nothing needs joining at render time.

sections.meta: Counts, licence, provenance rules, and this guide.
sections.ui: Pre-assembled views: generations, periods, timeline, milestones, highlights, facets, coverage. Start here for layout work.
sections.entities: Canonical records exactly as stored in data/*.json.
sections.graph: Flat nodes/edges with human-readable labels on every endpoint. For force-directed or matrix network views.
sections.entityDetail: Denormalized per-entity bundles: discography, labels, crews, songs, events, relations, resolved sources. Keyed by entity id.
sections.schema: Field definitions and data rules from schema/schema.json.

safety: Read entities.artists[].identityStatus before rendering any person. "pseudonym" and "anonymised" mean the identity is deliberately withheld - by the artist, or because publication would endanger them. Do not attempt to resolve one, do not merge two records to "fix" a near-match, and do not pair a pseudonym with a real name inferred from a producer credit, a shared surname or a common collaborator.

Some artists in this dataset are deceased, imprisoned, or executed. Phyo Zeya Thaw was executed on 25 July 2022; Byu Har is serving a 20-year sentence from August 2023; Lil Cado is deceased. Their records carry only what press has published. Do not add family or biographical detail beyond the cited sources.

Several post-coup releases and events were documented under conditions of surveillance and risk. A Telegram or Facebook channel that carried music may also be the channel that doxed someone. Do not characterise any platform as safe.

event "ev-raj-dickcouncil-party-2021" and the DICKCOUNCIL release were produced during a national internet shutdown. Distribution events in this period are evidence of circumstance, not just of promotion.
renderingHints: entities.artists and ui.generations are the primary navigation: group by generation, or by city (mostly Yangon, with Mandalay central to the fourth generation).

ui.generations[] each carry a `basis` field. 1-3 are `sourced` (the citations enumerate them). 4 and 5 are `asserted`: artist- and press-asserted framing, not a sourced taxonomy. Style them differently and never merge them with 1-3 without a visible qualifier.

ui.periods is the coarser editorial spine (c. 1994-2026) and is NOT the same axis as ui.generations. Periods reach past 2010; generations stop at "present" in the 3G label. Keep them distinct in the UI.
ui.periods[].unlinkedNames lists acts the sources name that have no entity record yet. Render them with a qualifier, never silently drop them.
ui.timeline is pre-sorted by year; render as a vertical or horizontal chronology.
entityDetail["acid"] and entityDetail["sai-sai-kham-leng"] are the two deepest profiles and make good hero/detail pages.
graph.edges[].status and .confidence let you dim unverified links without extra lookups.
ui.facets.activeByYear is a ready-made activity series for a chart.
Sort any people-facing list by year; id slugs are for keys only, never for display.
Burmese-script aliases live in entities.artists[].aliases - keep them, do not transliterate.

READ entities.artists[].identityStatus BEFORE building a people-facing list. Most records have no published real name, and post-coup acts are often deliberate pseudonyms. Do not attempt to resolve a pseudonym, and never pair one with a guessed name.

ui.coverage is an explicit inventory of gaps: real-name coverage, unknown activeFrom years, unlinked period names, and which generation buckets are asserted rather than sourced. Use it to show what is missing instead of implying completeness.
ui.facets.releasesWithoutYear and releases[].yearNote record re-release conflicts (e.g. Bo Htet's Heavy Weight, 2020 vs 2023). Show both dates; do not silently pick one.
The 2020s new wave is organised by LABEL, not crew or city. Navigate it via crews where kind is "label" and via artists[].labelIds. Presenting it as a crew scene would misrepresent its structure.

Diaspora is thin and real: ui.facets.artistBase and ui.coverage.artists.diasporaBase list every act with a non-Myanmar base. Seven of the nine countries checked have no documented rap scene at all - that absence is a finding, not an oversight.

ui.headline: Myanmar Hip-Hop: a sourced timeline of Yangon rap
ui.summary: From the first album in 2000 to a 2017 reunion show, this is an open, source-attributed archive of Myanmar hip-hop. Every fact links back to a citation, and every citation is marked verified, medium or low confidence.

editorial.positioning: An open Myanmar/Burmese hip-hop archive aiming to be an early public data resource. It does not claim to be the first website or first dataset.
editorial.methodNote: Two navigation axes ship and must not be conflated. ui.generations follows the labels the sources themselves use, and every bucket carries a `basis`: prehistory through 3rd are `sourced`, while 4th and New wave are `asserted` - artist- and press-asserted framing rather than a cited taxonomy. ui.periods is a coarser editorial spine running c. 1994-2026. First claims remain attributed and contested.
limitations: Romanisation varies: Anegga/Annaga; Phyo Zeya Thaw/Zayar Thaw; Sa Tin Chin/SaTin Gyin/Sa-Tin-Chein; Byauk-Oh/Byout-Oh; Examplz/Examplez; J-Me/JME; Bigg-Y/Bigg Y; G-Tone/G Tone; Bunny Phyoe/Bunny Phyo; Reload/ReLoad/RELOAD.
'First' is a source-attributed description, not a complete priority audit.
The 2001-05 roster is incomplete and unevenly sourced. G-Family's placement is contradictory.
The late-2000s 3G/VIP genealogy is especially tentative.

There is NO sourced fourth or fifth generation. The Burmese hip-hop encyclopedia article covers three generations and cannot support more. The 4G label rests on one artist statement - Yung Hugo telling HipHopDX in March 2022 'I'm fourth-generation' - plus MYANMORE's 2018 'a new hip hop generation has arrived'. The 'New wave' bucket is the archive's own editorial grouping of a label-network cohort, built from copyright structure and LIFTED scene reporting. Both are marked `basis: asserted` in the build output and should be presented as framing, not as established taxonomy.
The 4G/5G date boundary is the least certain thing in the dataset. The New wave bucket starts at 2018, which overlaps the fourth generation, because no source dates the shift.

Post-coup rosters are incomplete because aliases, concealed identities, displacement, platform removals and safety risk limit documentation. Thirteen artists are recorded as pseudonym or anonymised and 104 of 115 have no published real name. Do not attempt to resolve a pseudonym or pair one with a guessed name; VICE states outright that at least one alias was adopted to protect its user from the military.

Identity is a safety property, not a footnote. Read `identityStatus` before building any people-facing list. Phyo Zeya Thaw was executed on 25 July 2022 and Byu Har is serving 20 years from August 2023; both are recorded by stage name with their legal circumstances, and neither should be paired with family or biographical detail beyond what press has published.

The underground tape era is the best-documented decade in the archive and the worst-served by streaming platforms. Most of B-Clipz, M.R.C, Y.H.S, Wildboy, B-Lord Family and the Zay Ye' / Htet Yan / X-Boxin / G Fatt catalogues exists only in fan archives, most of which are now dead or hijacked domains. They are cited through web.archive.org only. The single highest-value remaining work is a systematic crawl of the ~23,000 archived mmhiphopchannel.com URLs and the myanmarmp3album.com 2008-2011 index, which together likely hold several hundred dated releases with tracklists that no streaming platform has catalogued.

MHC also reposted foreign albums - T.I., for instance - so any bulk ingestion of that archive needs a Myanmar-linkage filter. This archive is hand-curated and contains only verified Burmese-linked records.

Release dates on streaming platforms are unreliable for this scene, especially pre-2023. Several Yan releases carry 2014-2016 dates with 2024 copyright strings; Bo Htet's Heavy Weight appears as both 2020 and 2023; Yung Hugo's Make Karen Great Again slipped from July 2022 to February 2023. Affected records carry a `yearNote` and both values are preserved rather than resolved.

Where sources disagree, the disagreement is kept. DICKCOUNCIL is 12 tracks per Bandcamp and HipHopDX but '11 songs by 15 rappers' per RAJ's own statement; the likely reconciliation is an inference and is not asserted. GRACEe and Grace are separate platform entities and are not merged. Yair Yint Aung has two platform artist ids. Rap Against Junta is described by press as having a founder and by itself as having none.

Diaspora coverage is thin and the absences are real findings, not gaps in the search. Of nine countries checked, only Thailand/Chiang Mai has a documented rap scene and it is documented by a single outlet (DVB). The US has artist-level traces. India, Malaysia, Singapore, Japan, South Korea, Australia and the UK have no documented Burmese rap scene at all. The reason is most likely that the scenes are small, new, undocumented, or documented in Burmese- and Thai-language sources this project has not reached.

Burmese-language research is the single largest methodological hole. The strongest material for the tape era and the post-coup scene is Burmese-language, and the search tooling available here could not run Burmese queries productively; what was gathered came from crawling known domains and the Wayback CDX index. A dedicated Burmese search, and Facebook-page recovery for the archived fan pages, would likely change the dataset substantially.

Music press coverage of this scene is very thin. Nothing was found in Bandcamp Daily, OkayAfrica, The Fader, Pitchfork, Noisey or Rolling Stone, and no article was found in Frontier Myanmar, Myanmar Now, The Diplomat or Nikkei Asia. The absence of international music-press attention is itself a documented characteristic of the scene.

Identity is contested for several acts. NAY has two competing real-name candidates in platform credits and appears to be two roles at once (artist and mastering engineer); 223 was a trio of Yungpunch, Lil Cado and Zero, separated in 2021, and which two remain is unverified; the Apple Music Triple Edge is not established to be the Chiang Mai group and is kept separate; the 'KYI' credit is not established as Kan Kyi; TOXIC's Myanmar linkage rests on a single joint release; Bo Gyi remains unresearchable.

Some acts named in the sources reached the archive from the pop or mainstream sphere rather than the underground tape circuit - Sophia Everest via Myanmar Idol, Warso Moe Oo via Shwe FM, Ni Ni Khin Zaw as a pop artist. They appear in period `artistNames` rather than being promoted to artist records, so the underground framing is not silently widened.

Streaming-platform genre fields are metadata, not stylistic claims, and several are wrong: Adjustor is tagged Pop, Mossberg Arki has a track tagged Folk and another UK Hip-Hop, blazy's Zing is tagged Electronic. Genre in this dataset is recorded only where a cited source states it.

AI-generated music-analytics aggregators (musicmetricsvault, sounddrain, viberate) publish fabricated prose and invented listener figures and have poisoned parts of the record. Viberate's bio claims Lil Kee Boi is from South Korea - he is from Bago and based in Munich, and his own YouTube channel metadata is the likely source of the error. These sites are excluded from the source list and must never be cited. Pirate MP3 scrapers such as pologi.org are useful only as lead generators; facts from them were re-verified against Apple Music, Spotify or Shazam before use.

Platform artist pages are ambiguous for generic names. Numeric platform ids are recorded in the source records so collisions can be disambiguated: 28, SLAMM, blazy, Wink, Peachy and TOXIC all have unrelated same-name artists.

Several cited sources are offline. HipHopDX has been shut down and its articles are cited through web.archive.org; the Global Voices slug in an earlier revision was misspelled; DVB is the only outlet with sustained coverage of MOB Party. A dead URL is not grounds for dropping a well-evidenced fact, so `archivedUrl` carries the readable copy.
The archive does not claim that hip-hop changed public opinion or political outcomes. The evidence supports solidarity and mobilization among participants, not a measured causal effect.

Image assets are editorial reference images with credits and source links. They are not represented as public-domain assets; verify permission before redistribution. Credits live in data/images.json and per-period captions in data/periods.json, because one image file is captioned differently in different periods.

periods.label: Precursors + ACID breakthrough
periods.summary: Evidence supports a precursor phase around Myo Kyawt Myaing and late-1990s Yangon nightclub culture. ACID's 2000 Sa Tin Chin / Beginning is the widely reported breakthrough, but 'first' remains an attributed claim, not an exhaustive proof.
eventNotes: Late-1990s ACID nightclub origins
2000 - Sa Tin Chin / Beginning
facts: Htein Lin's historical account calls Myo Kyawt Myaing generally considered Burmese rap's godfather, while Apple Music displays a 1994 rap-labelled catalogue date that still needs original-release verification.
Multiple reputable retrospective sources date ACID's Sa Tin Chin / SaTin Gyin / Sa-Tin-Chein (Beginning) to 2000 and describe it as an immediate, chart-leading landmark.
ACID's four-member founding line-up is reported as Anegga/Annaga, Hein Zaw, Yan Yan Chan, and Phyo Zeya Thaw/Zayar Thaw.

periods.label: Underground consolidation
periods.summary: A youth-facing underground ecology grew under censorship. 'Second generation' is retained as a retrospective community label, not a fixed canon. Snare/Nay Win offers the clearest date-specific DIY release trail.
eventNotes: 2001 - Snare's 40-copy home album
2005 - Hip Hop Vibration VCD account
facts: Nay Win says Snare formed in 2000 and recorded a 40-copy unofficial home album in 2001 with a computer microphone.
Nay Win says arrests around 2003-04 disrupted Snare's next project, and describes a 2005 Hip Hop Vibration VCD release; the solo/group credit remains unresolved.
The recurring 9mm / Project-1 / Firecracker / Examplz / On-Track / Cyclone / M.H.A. roster comes mostly from community or tertiary histories and still needs act-by-act primary verification.

periods.label: 3G claims + mixed circulation
periods.summary: Late-2000s rap circulated through home-recorded demos, bootlegs, live shows and web video while official channels remained censored. 'Third generation' is a self-applied/secondary label, not a settled canon, and the same period is where the underground tape ecosystem becomes visible in the archive: B-Clipz, M.R.C and the Y.H.S studio in Yangon, Wildboy in Mandalay, and a proliferation of mixtapes and VCDs that no streaming platform has ever catalogued.
eventNotes: 2007 - Generation Wave forms after the Saffron Revolution crackdown
2009-2013 - Wildboy active in Mandalay; Wildboyz mixtape Feb 2013
2010 - Never Give Up video / activist music
2011-2014 - B-Clipz, M.R.C and Y.H.S release mixtapes and songs in Yangon
facts: A 2010 scholarly account documents near-weekly cool-season shows, stage-show bootlegs, home demos, and uploads to Burmesemtv.com - a mixed ecology, not a streaming-first scene.
The specific late-2006 third-generation self-identification and VIP/Rock$tar roster are weakly sourced; the archive keeps those names visibly qualified.
Generation Wave was an adjacent pro-democracy youth network using music, graffiti and pamphlets. It should not be collapsed into every third-wave rap act.

B-Clipz, formed in Yangon in August 2008 with nine members, never released an album: Aung Ye' Htike reports the group circulated songs plus planned mixtapes, and that he produced around 20 songs in 2011 alone. Mandalay's Wildboy released a 12-track mixtape in February 2013.

The archived fan channels that catalogued this era - Myanmar Hip Hop Channel, the Myanmar Hip Hop Underground blog and myanmarmp3album.com - are the only source for most of these releases. Several of those domains are now dead or hijacked and are cited through web.archive.org only.

periods.label: Reform era, underground tape scene and the fourth generation
periods.kicker: TAPES, PARKS, AND THE LABEL YEARS
periods.summary: The 2012 end of pre-publication censorship widened room for music, but legal restrictions, self-censorship, permits and weak venues remained. This is also the decade the underground tape scene is best documented: Mandalay's Wildboy produced Oasix and Y-Zet, while Yangon ran on mixtapes, VCDs and small live platforms such as Jam It! and the Full Stop shows. By 2017 a fourth generation had arrived in the form of Yung Hugo, X-Boxin, Htet Yan, Zay Ye' and the BG18 circle, and the live scene had contracted from big-hotel bills to park shows and hotel residencies.
eventNotes: 2012 - pre-publication media censorship ends
2012 - Jam It! first show, Kan Daw Gyi Park
2015 - 'Pyaw San Par' duo album; nationwide recognition
2016 - FIRST STEP at Myaw Sin Island; Monsoon II at the Yangon International Hotel; Straight Outta Yangon Round 3
2017 - Straight Outta Yangon Chapter 2, ACID reunion; Y-Zet promotion in Mandalay turns violent
2018 - X-Boxin album 99; Oasix album 1992; Htet Yan and Thar Thar's 'Nway Thwar Tal'
2019 - Break the Night, French Institute Yangon; Adjustor's Compoptable
facts: BBC and Human Rights Watch date the end of pre-publication media censorship to 20 August 2012, while also documenting continued restrictive laws and self-censorship.

Oasix and Y-Zet both came out of Mandalay's Wildboy crew, then released the duet album 'Pyaw San Par' on 24 December 2015, which gave Oasix nationwide recognition. Oasix's own biography titles his 2009-2013 phase 'Career beginnings in underground'.

Jam It!, founded by Eaiddhi and Ye Ngwe Soe, started as an acoustic gig in Kan Daw Gyi Park in late 2012 and had run 20+ gigs across Yangon and Mandalay by 2015 with 40+ acts, cross-genre with punk, metal and live graffiti. It is the best-documented underground live platform in the archive.

Yung Hugo's Make Karen Great Again (2023) is a Karen-language album, marking ethnic-language rap as distinct from the Yangon-centre framing of earlier periods. He describes 2010-2015 as 'the golden age of hip hop' but says he was told there were no shows, and wants to rebuild it.

The live scene contracted rather than disappeared: free park shows at Myaw Sin Island in 2016 sat alongside paid hotel residencies, and the 2017 Y-Zet album promotion in Mandalay turned violent, killing a 19-year-old.

The Global Voices-era reporting on Y.A.K., Ko Minn and Jam It! documents a scene more regional and self-organised than a single Yangon mainstream. Several acts named in this period came from the pop or mainstream sphere rather than the underground tape circuit; the archive keeps that distinction visible in artistNames rather than promoting them.

The earliest record here is physical: Jimmy Jacobs handed out CDs and cassettes at his shows when internet access in Myanmar was still limited, which is the clearest single document of the distribution era the fourth generation came out of.

periods.label: Post-coup resistance + current scene
periods.summary: After the 1 February 2021 coup, rap became the most visible form of cultural resistance, and the scene split along three lines at once. Rap Against Junta grew from street concerts in Yangon and released DICKCOUNCIL in October 2021 while the country had no reliable internet. The BG18 label circle in Yangon carried on releasing - Adjustor, GRACEe, Yung Hugo - and Yung Hugo's 2023 Make Karen Great Again was a Karen-language album. A diaspora strand moved to Chiang Mai, where Kan Kyi organises MOB Party, and to Indianapolis, where Vanzzzo released 'Rebel (Save Myanmar)'. Separately, a new wave organised by label rather than crew took hold in Yangon, from Lil Kee Boi's Bago-to-Munich trap through 223, Ah Sar, Myat Amara Maung and Reload. No canonical 2021-2026 generation is asserted, and the sources do not agree on one.
eventNotes: 2021-02 - first RAJ street show, Yangon
2021-10-21 - DICKCOUNCIL listening party, streamed on YouTube
2022-07-25 - Phyo Zeya Thaw executed; 'Generation Driven by Faith' released posthumously 2023
2023-08-24 - Byu Har sentenced to 20 years
2024-11-30 and 2025-11-29 - MOB Party, Chiang Mai
2025-11-02 - Overflow Music Festival, Yangon; 16 charged
facts: The 1 February 2021 coup was followed within weeks by dozens of anti-military tracks across Facebook, YouTube and SoundCloud; Facebook itself was blocked 4-7 February 2021 and the country then lost the internet for weeks, with 46 consecutive nights of wireless blackout before a full national cut from 1 April.

Rap Against Junta is best represented as a decentralised alliance of MCs, producers, DJs, sound engineers, dancers, promoters, organisers and graffiti artists, insisting 'We are all leaders'. VICE names Osho - an alias adopted to protect his identity - as the originator. Its DICKCOUNCIL track count is genuinely disputed: Bandcamp and HipHopDX say 12, RAJ's own statement says 11 songs by 15 rappers, and the archive preserves both.

Byu Har, described by the BBC as one of Myanmar's biggest hip-hop artists, was arrested in May 2023 after a Facebook Live criticising power cuts and sentenced to 20 years in August. He is not a member of Rap Against Junta.

DVB documents MOB Party in Chiang Mai in 2024 and 2025 with Thai, Myanmar and international participation. Of nine countries checked for a Burmese rap scene, only Thailand has a documented one and it is documented by a single outlet; seven have nothing at all, which is a finding rather than an oversight.

The 2020s new wave is organised by label rather than crew or city: Billionaire Minds Group dominates, with Eagle Element and b4 Records alongside it. Drill and Jersey Club are the new sounds, per LIFTED's 2023 scene report.

Phyo Zeya Thaw, ACID co-founder and Generation Wave member, was executed on 25 July 2022. Rap Against Junta later released his unfinished 'Generation Driven by Faith', built around a prison voice note in which he says he never completed it.

generations.label: Precursors
generations.summary: The groundwork laid before the first records: Myo Kyawt Myaing performing from 1988, and Sai Sai Kham Leng releasing Chocolate Yaung Yayge Einmet in 2000.

generations.label: 1st generation
generations.summary: The first wave. Acid released Beginning (Sa-Tin-Gyin) in 2000, Burma's first hip-hop album, and topped the domestic charts for over two months. Theory, NS and Too Big followed.

generations.label: 2nd generation
generations.summary: The scene consolidates: 9mm, Project-1, Byauk-Oh, Examplz, G-Family, On-Track, L.E.E, Cyclone, plus the M.H.A. association and solo acts J-Me, Bigg-Y and G-Tone. Snare and the Rap Master Nay Win anchor Snare.

generations.label: 3rd generation
generations.summary: A new wave from late 2006: Jouk Jack, Kyaw Htut Swe, VIP / Rock$tar, Hlwan Paing, Ah Boy and Htein Win P Crew. In late 2008 and early 2009 many third-generation groups released their sample albums.

generations.label: 4th generation
generations.summary: The underground-tape generation, and the first cohort to reach the mainstream. Mandalay's Wildboy crew produced Oasix and Y-Zet; Yangon's tape and VCD circuit ran through B-Clipz, MRC, Y.H.S and B-Lord Family, with a parallel live scene at Jam It! and the Full Stop shows. Oasix and Y-Zet came out of Wildboy; Htet Yan, X-Boxin, Zay Ye', Bo Htet, G Fatt and Floke Rose followed, and Yung Hugo's Make Karen Great Again (2023) marks ethnic-language rap as a fourth-generation marker. Trap took years to be accepted: Yung Hugo, "It has only been a few years since people accepted trap music here."
generations.caveat: No cited source enumerates a fourth generation. The label is artist-asserted (Yung Hugo: "I'm fourth-generation") and press-asserted (MYANMORE, 2018). Wikipedia calling Ah Boy a "pioneer of the third generation" implies a fourth is a recognised category, but does not list one.

generations.label: New wave
generations.summary: A platform-native generation organised by label rather than crew or city. Billionaire Minds Group is the dominant copyright network across the 2023-2026 cohort, with Eagle Element (Lil Kee Boi, Ah Sar) and b4 Records (Wink, bkho bain) alongside it. The sound is trap, drill and Jersey Club: LIFTED's 2023 scene report highlights a four-way drill cut and a Jersey Club collaboration with 223. Two diaspora strands run through it - Lil Kee Boi from Bago to Munich, and Myat Amara Maung, Reload and Yan working out of the BMG network. The names themselves call it "Burma's new wave rap scene".
generations.caveat: An editorial grouping, not a cited taxonomy. Built from label structure and LIFTED scene reporting rather than from any source that lists a fifth generation. The 2018-2022 boundary overlaps the fourth generation and is the least certain date in this table.

beefIsNotBeef.finding: A systematic sweep of ~23,000 archived fan-catalogue URLs found that "beef" in Burmese hip hop is overwhelmingly a GENRE LABEL and a SONG TITLE, not a documented grievance. Every archived post whose slug contains "beef" is a multi-artist posse cut, and not one names a target. One is titled "Beef History" and is performed by four members of the same crew together.
beefIsNotBeef.implication: Do not build a feud-view by matching on the word "beef". Use data/disputes.json, where a claim, a target and evidence exist.

vsUsuallyMeansCollaboration.finding: "vs" overwhelmingly means a same-track collaboration or a battle recording rather than a feud. Verified examples: "Jouk Jack Vs. Kyaw Htut Swe" is a 7-track mixtape by two members of the same group; "J Ki Vs G Fatt" is a feature on a track about a lover's quarrel; "G Tone Vs ကက္က" is a remix.
vsUsuallyMeansCollaboration.implication: Treat a "vs" title as a credit fact, never as evidence of rivalry.

dissIsRarelyNamed.finding: "diss" is nearly absent as a naming convention, which is the opposite of expectation: across 23,033 archived URLs only two contain it, and one of those is entirely produced and written by the artist's own crew. The scene absorbed the battle as a PERFORMANCE FORM rather than a named-feud genre - burying a diss in a cypher was the norm.
dissIsRarelyNamed.implication: A dispute with no diss track on the record is not a contradiction of the pattern here.

hateIsAFalsePositive.finding: "hate" is the dominant keyword in these archives and is about 90% romantic. Slugs like "i-hate-u", "love-to-hate" and "keep-calm-coz-i-hate-u" are love songs. Any keyword classifier over this corpus will drown in them.

theRealMarker.finding: The genuine Burmese marker for a public dispute is ရေးကောက်, used as a verb, and a second marker is တာဝန်မကျေခဲ့မှု ("not fulfilling one's duty") - which is how the Ah Boy departure from VIP was reported. The pattern to search for is a Latin-alphabet post title paired with a Burmese subtitle, e.g. "Doubt Battle (သံသယတိုက္ပြဲ)", glossed as "onslaught/criticism + big fight".

pre2011TheTargetWasTheState.finding: Before 2011 the dispute was with the state, not between artists. Independent reporting describes the 2007-08 period as one in which artists were slandered, banned and arrested on stage for their lyrics; Acid's Beginning had 16 tracks of which the censor board passed 11; Zayar Thaw said "we made 16 songs, but the censorship board only passed 11".
pre2011TheTargetWasTheState.implication: For the earliest era, legal/censorship records absorb what a Western archive would file as beefs.

thePivot.finding: The one clean beef analogue in the archive is a deliberate transfer of the battle form onto the state. DICKCOUNCIL producer Ko Aye Win, a former battler, told Insight Myanmar in December 2021: "Before the coup I was a B-Boy, I liked to battle a lot. But not anymore... So I thought, how about we switch the arrow direction in Dickcouncil, to take on the military junta and Min Aung Hlaing or whoever, like every tyrant across the globe!"
thePivot.implication: The target of the adversarial form migrated from other rappers to the regime. That migration is the pivot point of the whole dataset.

veiledDiss.finding: Where a real personal dispute did surface, the mechanism was the veiled diss. Bobby Soxer's 2022 track is titled "No Right to Speak Without Naming Names" (နာမည်တပ်ပြီးပြောပိုင့်ခွင့်မရှိ) - the title itself announces the indirectness, and it deliberately does not name its target.

creditDisputesAreAbsent.finding: A credit dispute here is usually not a quarrel between artists but an ABSENT LEGAL CATEGORY. Thar Si Thaw of the Myanmar Music Association testified to VOA in 2016 that "the existing laws cannot give the necessary protection". Phyo Layy writes invisibly as a lyricist for other artists with no public credit and no documented grievance. A specific investigation of credit disputes around 99 Symphony's INTERNATION and Phyo Layy found no dispute exists at all - he does not appear in that album's writer credits.

selfPolicing.finding: The scene self-polices on two axes, both aimed at the industry rather than at rivals: underground against mainstream (artists going commercial were criticised as "selling out", with Sai Sai Kham Leng the named example), and authenticity-by-knowledge - Kyaw Htut Swe remarks that people who only know the music from sample CDs are not real participants.
selfPolicing.implication: Neither axis is a documented feud between named individuals. Do not code them as disputes.

corrections: The Y-Zet concert death of June 2017 is NOT a beef killing. The fight began with accidental elbowing while dancing at a free show, six years after the "Shwee Die" diss. Do not link them.

There is no documented beef between Y-Zet and Oasix or Mg Moe Aung. Every source shows them as closest collaborators and duo album partners; the archive's earlier note implying one has been retracted. The documented diss runs outward, to Hlwan Paing.
G-Tone's November 2007 sanction was a one-year ban by the Myanmar Music Association, not an arrest, and not 2008. Coconuts (2015) garbles it as a 2008 arrest.
Rock$tar and VIP are ONE group with two names, not two groups. The archive previously carried them separately; the real event is Ah Boy's departure.
"Pyaw San Par" and "ပြောစမ်းပါ" are the same Dec 2015 Oasix & Y-Zet album under two titles. "1992" is Oasix's birth year, not a release.
Rappler's investigation of the Telegram doxing that led to Byu Har's arrest is dated 22 August 2023, not March 2025, and the arrest was May 2023.
The Overflow Music Festival charges are ss. 505-A, 294 and 114 per the police statement, not 505(b).
Frenzo is a production company owned by Sai Sai Kham Leng, not a collective.
HEIN HTET ZAW, HOT and OT THE CROC are ONE artist, not two or three. And ဦးတိုက် is not his Burmese name: ဦး is the honorific "U", making it read as "U Toik", and no source uses it.

entries.detail: Parking lot at Cool Muang Coffee near Tha Phae Gate, Chiang Mai. Thai, Myanmar and international participation. Raises funds for children who remain stateless and are at risk due to displacement and lack of access to education. entries.title: RK Showdown (Mandalay earthquake charity hip-hop show)
entries.detail: Featuring Myo Kyawt Myaing, Yatha, G-Tone, Jouk Jack and Sandy Myint Lwin. RARE EVIDENCE OF A YANGON-MANDALAY CO-BILL: four of the five performers are Yangon acts appearing in Mandalay, which is the clearest documented instance of cross-city traffic in the archive. G-Tone's presence is notable given his 2007 performance ban.

entries.title: Cover Club Buddha-song DJ set (prosecuted)
entries.detail: 1-2am. Three DJs played a DJ mix of 'Buddham Saranam Gacchami' and danced in a way reported as disrespecting Buddhism. Charged under s.505(a), case (P)214/2025, Myoma PS; arrested 11 and 13 Sept 2025. Not a rap event - recorded because it is the archive's only documented Mandalay prosecution of a music performer, and because the same s.505(a) architecture catches rappers. Performer names are deliberately not entered as artist records.

entries.title: Overflow Music Festival
entries.detail: Eastern Yangon Event Park. bkho bain (as Thein Min Htike) and Wink (as Ye Wint Aung, 'Bala') performed material using obscene language and distributed condoms. Police arrested participants between 5 and 6 Nov; 16 people were charged under Myanmar Penal Code ss. 505(b) and 294, with arrests in Tamwe, Yankin and Thingangyun townships. One of the clearest documented instances of legal repression of a live hip-hop event.

entries.title: MOB Party (4th annual)
entries.detail: Democrazy!, Chiang Mai. Thai headliner Elevenfinger was released from prison in Thailand shortly before this edition.

entries.title: 4 Elements residency exhibition (A New Burma)
entries.detail: Infra Practice Chiang Mai, 21-24 May 2026, Norway-backed. A New Burma, founded by Hnin Win, has worked with 100+ artists since 2022 and has shown in Bangkok, London, Manchester and Melbourne. Not rap-specific, but the nearest thing the diaspora has to scene infrastructure.

entries.title: SCARR - Resilience Arts Exhibition
entries.detail: Chiang Mai, 27-28 June 2026. 20 Myanmar artists, many living in hiding or on precarious legal status in Thailand; co-organised with Artists' Shelter. SAFETY: participants are deliberately unnamed in the source and one is credited only as 'Harry'. Do not attempt to identify. Recorded as context for the conditions the exile scene works under, not as a hip-hop event.

milestones.title: Myo Kyawt Myaing performing
milestones.text: The earliest figure recorded in the archive as active, treated as a pioneer of Burmese hip-hop.

milestones.title: Acid releases Burma's first hip-hop album
milestones.text: Beginning (Sa-Tin-Gyin) by Acid, founded by Phyo Zeya Thaw, Annaga, Hein Zaw and Yan Yan Chan, topped the Burmese charts for more than two months.

milestones.title: Sai Sai Kham Leng debuts
milestones.text: Debut album Chocolate Yaung Yayge Einmet, followed in 2001 by Thangegyin Myar Swar, which made him a star.

milestones.title: "One Nal Mhat Tan" hits number one
milestones.text: The track from February Mhat Tann reached number one in Myanmar.

milestones.title: Sai Sai Birthday Show begins
milestones.text: Annual outdoor concert held every 10 April from 2004, a fixture of the Yangon calendar.

milestones.title: Third generation emerges
milestones.text: From late 2006 a new wave appears: Jouk Jack, Kyaw Htut Swe, VIP / Rock$tar, Hlwan Paing.

milestones.title: Generation Wave youth movement
milestones.text: Phyo Zeya Thaw is documented as part of Generation Wave, a youth movement rather than a rap group.

milestones.title: Oasix releases his first solo mixtape
milestones.text: While still a university student and a member of Mandalay crew Wildboy, Oasix released "The First", then "The Running" in 2013. His Wikipedia biography titles the phase "2009-2013: Career beginnings in underground", which makes this the archive's clearest documented pipeline from the underground tape scene to the mainstream.

milestones.title: Jam It! begins as an acoustic gig in Kan Daw Gyi Park
milestones.text: Eaiddhi and Ye Ngwe Soe started Jam It! as an acoustic show late 2012. By 2015 it had run 20+ gigs across Yangon and Mandalay with 40+ acts, booking punk, hard rock, metal and hip hop on the same bill alongside live graffiti artists - the best-documented underground live platform in the archive.

milestones.title: Oasix reaches nationwide recognition
milestones.text: The duet album "Pyaw San Par (Just say it)" with Y-Zet, released 24 December 2015, brought nationwide recognition, with hit songs and a run of commercial and concert work across Myanmar. Oasix's solo album "1992" followed in December 2018.

milestones.title: Acid reunion at The Clubhouse
milestones.text: Straight Outta Yangon: Chapter 2, an ACID reunion show in Yangon, and the subject of Insight Myanmar episode 604.

milestones.title: "Nway Thwar Tal" breaks out on TikTok
milestones.text: The #1 single from Htet Yan and Thar Thar's album "Shae Mhi Nout Mhi" went viral on TikTok in early 2019 with more than 50,000 user videos, and was later sampled in an Imagine Dragons melody. The clearest documented case of a short-form-video breakout carrying a Burmese underground act into the mainstream.

milestones.title: The coup and the resistance scene
milestones.text: After the 1 February 2021 coup, rap became the most visible form of cultural resistance. Rap Against Junta formed from street concerts in Yangon, releasing DICKCOUNCIL in October 2021; Louz Xa Lone released "The Voices" on Facebook on 3 February; Vanzzzo, in Indianapolis, released "Rebel (Save Myanmar)" in March. Myanmar then cut the internet for weeks, which pushed the scene onto Bandcamp, YouTube and Spotify - making the international platforms the de facto archive of the movement.

milestones.title: Phyo Zeya Thaw executed; his unfinished track released posthumously
milestones.text: ACID co-founder and Generation Wave member Phyo Zeya Thaw was executed on 25 July 2022, aged 41 - reported as the first use of capital punishment in Myanmar in decades. In 2023 Rap Against Junta released his unfinished "Generation Driven by Faith", built around a voice note in which he says he wrote the bars in prison and never completed them. A 2026 documentary, "The Rapper and the Junta" by Thomas Dandois, is about him.

milestones.title: Byu Har sentenced to 20 years
milestones.text: The rapper Byu Har, described by the BBC as one of Myanmar's biggest hip-hop artists and the son of songwriter Naing Myanmar, was arrested on 24 May 2023 after a Facebook Live criticising power cuts. He was held at North Dagon Police Station and sentenced to 20 years on 24 August 2023. Press reports charge incitement under Penal Code art. 505(a) and a treason statute, but the specific conviction was not confirmed at the time of reporting. He is not a member of Rap Against Junta.

milestones.title: MOB Party documents the Chiang Mai exile scene
milestones.text: The third MOB Party, held 30 November 2024 at a parking lot near Tha Phae Gate in Chiang Mai, brought together Thai, Myanmar and international artists. Organiser Kan Kyi frames the event as building artist relations across Southeast Asia and raising funds for stateless children at risk from displacement. DVB is the only outlet with a sustained record of this scene.

milestones.title: Sixteen charged after the Overflow Music Festival
milestones.text: bkho bain and Wink performed at the Overflow Music Festival at Eastern Yangon Event Park on 2 November 2025. Police arrested participants between 5 and 6 November and charged 16 people under Myanmar Penal Code ss. 505(b) and 294, with arrests across three Yangon townships. One of the clearest documented instances of legal repression of a live hip-hop event.

undergroundToMainstream.note: Oasix and Y-Zet both began in the same Mandalay underground crew and both reached the mainstream; Oasix's debut album was a duet with Y-Zet.

artists.name: Phyo Zeya Thaw
artists.note: ACID co-founder and Generation Wave member. Served six years, released 17 May 2011. Arrested Nov 2021 for alleged 'terrorist attacks' and EXECUTED 25 July 2022 aged 41 - reported as the first use of capital punishment in Myanmar in decades. A 2026 documentary, 'The Rapper and the Junta' by Thomas Dandois, is about him.

artists.name: Ah Boy
artists.note: Born Kyaw Phyo Tun on 13 Jan 1986 in Myeik, Tanintharyi Division, to a Sino-Mon family; family moved to Yangon when he was 3. Lead vocalist of Rock$tar from 2002, and Wikipedia calls him a 'pioneer of the third generation of Burmese hip hop' - which implies a fourth generation is a recognised category. Solo debut album Ta Yoke Tan (Chinatown) 2007. 'A Ngweh A That Myar' (with ChanMyae MgCho) hit #1 on the JOOX top 100 in 2020 and won the JOOX 2020 Popular Song Award. MEMBERSHIP: lead vocalist of VIP (Rock$tar) from its 2007 formation, and a former member. His exit is the group's documented event; a Feb 2013 Burmese headline implies a grievance about him not fulfilling his role rather than a rupture. Wikipedia calls him a 'pioneer of the third generation of Burmese hip hop', which implies a fourth is a recognised category.

artists.name: Oasix
artists.note: The clearest documented underground-to-mainstream path in the archive: Wildboy member from 2009, then a solo career. Wikipedia's own career section is titled '2009-2013: Career beginnings in underground'. Father Tun Wai was a Mandalay District court judge. His Dec 2015 duet album appears under two titles ('Pyaw San Par' in Wikipedia, ပြောစမ်းပါ in the fan archive); the archive records one release with both titles. '1992' is his birth year.

artists.name: Y-Zet
artists.note: Long-running Wildboy member and Oasix's duet partner. Born 28 May 1989 in Pyin Oo Lwin, Mandalay REGION - not Mandalay city; school BEHS No. 4 Pyin Oo Lwin, chemistry at Yadanabon University, dropped out 2008. Joined Wildboy 2011. His 2017 album promotion in Mandalay turned violent and a 19-year-old died. INTERVIEWED BY IDEA Magazine, Aug 2017. NO BEEF WITH OASIX OR MG MOE AUNG: the archive's earlier note implying one is retracted - every source shows them as closest collaborators and duo partners, and the documented diss runs outward, not between them.

artists.name: Zay Ye'
artists.note: Billed with an 'MC' prefix in a 2010 interview. Describes having no industry connections, self-financing early recordings and selling VIP samples for cash, with thousands of songs still unreleased. Bursts on streaming via a 37-song 'Best of Myanmar Hip Hop' playlist.

artists.name: Bo Htet
artists.note: Appears in a 2018 Coconuts freestyle-battle lineup.

artists.name: Htet Yan
artists.note: From Meiktila, moved to Yangon. Ran a four-album collective with Shwe Htoo, Lil'Z and X-Box. 'Nway Thwar Tal' (2018) went viral on TikTok in early 2019 with 50,000+ user videos. NOTE: an album called 'Thu' is NOT verified; the documented 2016 second album is 'October 18'.

artists.name: X-Boxin
artists.note: Born in Myeik, raised Yangon. Sharpened his rhyme 'at Yangon's underground freestyle competitions' (self-description). Myanmar Music Award for Best Young Rap Artist, 2014. The connective tissue across the 4G, BG18 and 2020s label scenes.

artists.name: Phyo Layy
artists.note: Snare member from the group's formation in 2000, later solo. From Kyaukmyaung, Yangon. Also a lyricist for Sandi Myint Lwin, Wine Su Khaing Thein and Warso Moe Oo. Snare is a group record in artists.json, not a crew, so the membership is carried as a relationship rather than a crewId.

artists.name: G Fatt
artists.note: Underground origins before going mainstream. Won Best Hip Hop Album and Album of the Year at Major M 2018, and Artist of the Year 2018. First one-man show at Kandawgyi, Nov 2018.

artists.name: Floke Rose
artists.note: Won Voice of the Youth 2017. Deliberately solo: he says he avoided joining any hip-hop group. On the scene's battle culture: 'the local underground hip-hop scene has been usually packed with lyrics on the street, rap battles to boost one's egos, girls, parties'.

artists.name: Jimmy Jacobs
artists.note: Rapping from c. 2008; founded SME with Luffie in Dec 2009. He handed out CDs and cassettes at shows when internet access in Myanmar was still limited - a direct documentation of the physical-to-platform transition.

artists.name: 99 Symphony
artists.note: 'INTERNATION' (2024) carries a very large feature list including X-Boxin, Reload and JCZ. Origin city and background are not in any source found. The band's own release misspells the name as '9 Symphony'.

artists.name: Moe Htet (B+)
artists.note: Producer, rapper and writer. Wrote 'IDFC' (Sophia Everest and Sandy Myint Lwin), Best R&B Song at the Major M Music Awards 2018. 'Medusa' with Sophia Everest reached #1 on the Major M Local Top 30 in 2019.

artists.name: Yair Yint Aung
artists.note: The anchor act of the BG18 circle, active from 2013. CONFLICTED: Apple Music hosts him under two different artist ids (1528815375 and 1194944521), so part of his catalogue sits under a split page.

artists.name: JCZ
artists.note: Producer and artist in the BG18 circle; co-produced Yung Hugo's Sold Out mixtape with him.

artists.name: Eillie
artists.note: In the BG18 circle; released tracks on X-Boxin's W, Vol. 1 and features on 99 Symphony's INTERNATION.

artists.name: Bobby Soxer
artists.note: Duet partner of Hlwan Paing on 'Done Pyan (Rocket)' (2011), which won best music album from both Shwe FM and City FM; the 1M kyat gold prize was donated to orphans.

artists.name: Bunny Phyoe
artists.note: Spelled Bunny Phyoe / Bunny Phyo / Bunny Phyo across sources; one canonical form is used here. A 30-track unreleased collection circulated in 2010.

artists.name: G Latt
artists.note: Thin sourcing: confirmed on Phyo Layy's 2019 album and on a 2014 release. No bio, no city.

artists.name: Aung Ye' Htike
aliases: ေအာင္ရဲထိုက္
artists.note: B-Clipz founder. Reports producing c. 20 songs in 2011 and that the group never released an album, only songs plus planned mixtapes. Ran the MMHLS lyric-video channel.

artists.name: Eaiddhi
artists.note: Jam It! co-founder. Freelance sound engineer; previously of Married For The Pain and Side Effect.

artists.name: Ye Ngwe Soe
artists.note: Jam It! co-founder. No U Turn vocalist and guitarist from 2002; FM Bagan producer; Happy Three Friends studio.

artists.name: Lil Kee Boi
artists.note: Trap artist from Bago ('BGO'), based in Munich. Self-describes as recording from his room since 2021. Founder of Eagle Element, describes himself as CEO. 'Mother Teresa' with NAY is the breakout (12M+ YouTube views). DANGER: Viberate's AI-generated bio claims he is 'from South Korea' and YouTube channel metadata lists country KR; both are wrong and the Viberate page should never be cited.

Self-described 'Burmese Slime From Taungoo', founded 2019. Was a trio of Yungpunch, Lil Cado and Zero, all related; separated 2021 and is now a duo - which two survive is UNVERIFIED. Internal roles per official video credits: Yungpunch produces, Lil Cado mixes, NAY masters. Lil Cado is deceased by Dec 2025 and is billed '(Rip)'. LIFTED describes them as a duo on a Jersey Club beat.

artists.name: Ah Sar
artists.note: Born and raised Yangon, began making music at 15. Describes himself as part of 'Burma's new wave rap scene' and as Eagle Element's first early member. Two full-length releases in 2025. Possible label migration Eagle Element -> Billionaire Minds Group between May and Nov 2025, inferred from (P) strings and not explicitly documented.

artists.name: MURKIO
artists.note: Earliest verifiable release 2022. The most frequent collaborator in the new wave after Lil Kee Boi: appears with him, Ah Sar, Reload and Myat Amara Maung. One EP is credited jointly to A555H and MURKIO; whether A555H is Murkio, a duo or an alias is UNVERIFIED.

artists.name: Myat Amara Maung
artists.note: Long-running crossover act and the most consistent collaborator of Reload. 34.7K monthly listeners. CREDIBILITY WARNING: Viberate's bio ('pop musician from Singapore... catchy melodies') is AI-generated filler and Viberate lists her as Singaporean on no primary evidence; the Spotify/Singapore market association is recorded as base but the Singapore residency claim is NOT verified by any cited source.

artists.name: Reload
artists.note: Solo artist, not a collective or label - confirmed. Self-describes as 'Straight out of GTL', which could not be resolved to a city, region or crew. Collaborates with Myat Amara Maung, Louz Xa Lone, PHATKIDz, KN, Yan and Murkio. His only 'album' on Apple Music, 12 Yar Thi (2018), is credited jointly to Nay & Reload and is NOT a solo album.

artists.name: Mossberg Arki
artists.note: ONE artist, not 'Mossberg' plus 'Arki' - all releases including the self-labelled ones map to a single Apple Music id. The most substantial album/EP catalogue in the new wave: one album plus two EPs by 2026.

artists.name: Wink
artists.note: Rapper and producer/alt-leaning artist on b4 Records; principal collaborator of bkho bain. Credited as Ye Wint Aung ('Bala') in press. DANGER: name collision with Josh Wink (US house producer) and a Japanese act; the Spotify page showing 267.8K monthly listeners is NOT this artist (ours is 12zhECtz6sIwtvL5BMkLLp).

artists.name: bkho bain
artists.note: Real name from press. Debut album BLUE ON BLUE (2024) on FASTLANE, charted in Australia and Thailand. Performed with Wink at the Overflow Music Festival, Eastern Yangon, Nov 2025, after which 16 people were charged under Penal Code ss. 505(b) and 294 - one of the clearest documented state/legal interventions in the archive. Album length conflicts across sources (13 vs 14 tracks).

artists.name: Yan - ヤン
artists.note: Display name mixes Latin and Japanese katakana, but NO source confirms any Japan connection - do not infer one. CREDIBILITY WARNING: several Apple Music release dates for this artist read 2014-2016 while carrying (P) 2024 Billionaire Minds Group strings; these are re-release or data-entry artefacts, so activeFrom is NOT established.

artists.name: TOXIC
artists.note: Bills as the second half of 'Myat Amara Maung & TOXIC' with producer Ricky Pink. 15+ unrelated artists are named Toxic on Apple Music; no standalone page could be isolated, and Myanmar linkage rests entirely on one joint release. Thinly documented - treat existence as probable, not established.

artists.name: Peachy
artists.note: Debut-era act, closely linked to 28 and SLAMM - all three appear on multiple joint releases. Note Apple Music lists Peachy's primary genre as Pop while every release is tagged Hip-Hop/Rap.
Very young debut-era act: earliest release Dec 2025, one album in 2026. A purely numeric name is the most collision-prone in the dataset; the Myanmar Apple Music id is 1855905920.

artists.name: SLAMM
artists.note: Debut-era peer of 28 and Peachy. Name collision with a Korean hip-hop act (1351947938) and a Brazilian pop act; the Myanmar Apple Music id is 1875095188.

artists.name: blazy
artists.note: Singles only, no album or EP found. Marks the earliest of the Eagle Element circle. Name collision with a trance producer (1592114070) and others; the Myanmar Apple Music id is 1831078905.

artists.name: Elco Dakid
artists.note: Self-tags as 'Burmese rap'. Producer on the 7-way track 'Khow Khow Nam' (2026). Spotify shows 3,249 monthly listeners. Nearly all biographical fields are UNVERIFIED; two attribution lines on the Spotify page are ambiguous and are NOT recorded as a real name.

artists.name: Yungpunch
artists.note: From Taungoo; founding member and producer of 223. Now runs a self-released solo imprint. No album under his own name verified.

artists.name: Immad
artists.note: Featured by Ah Sar on FLY and PARTY. Chartmetric lists Thailand as primary market, but that is audience geography, NOT residence, so base is deliberately left null. Featured on The Lot Radio (Brooklyn) in Apr 2026, the only non-platform third-party confirmation found. CAUTION: unrelated 'Immad' results (Pakistani, Bangladeshi) are a constant collision risk.

artists.name: Ye' Lay
artists.note: Appears in the new-wave feature network: on Zay Ye' tracks, on J-Me's 'A Rel', and on a 2023 Zay Ye' compilation. The id 'yzl' was an internal placeholder; the canonical slug is now ye-lay. Thin sourcing - no bio, no city, no independent platform page isolated.

artists.name: Rap Against Junta
artists.note: Not a fixed roster. Self-description: 'an alliance of MCs, producers, DJs, sound engineers, dancers, promoters, organizers and graffiti artists' and 'We are all leaders.' Emerged from street concerts around the 1 Feb 2021 coup. YouTube channel joined 15 Mar 2021 and was originally used for scratch-DJ tutorials and short freestyles. Owns its Bandcatalogue because distribution inside Myanmar can be switched off. Also released Zayar Thaw's posthumous 'Generation Driven by Faith'.

artists.name: Osho
artists.note: VICE names Osho as the originator of the 'conscious musicians' network from which RAJ was assembled, aged 42 in 2023. PRESS EXPLICITLY STATES THIS IS AN ALIAS ADOPTED TO PROTECT HIS IDENTITY FROM THE MILITARY. Do not attempt to identify. Co-hosts a community and mental-health podcast with Sai Hlyan.

artists.name: Ko Aye Win
artists.note: Producer of DICKCOUNCIL; former B-boy and battler. Interviewed at length by Insight Myanmar in Dec 2021 on the album as a propaganda instrument.

artists.name: Be Amby
artists.note: DICKCOUNCIL contributor with a solo catalogue (Reason to Live 2022, Freedom to Dream 2023, Season to Sing 2025). The clearest RAJ-to-Chiang-Mai personnel bridge, via Triple Edge's 'BROKEN SPEAKER' (2024).

artists.name: Sai Hlyan
artists.note: Myanmar DJ living outside the country; co-hosts a community and mental-health podcast with Osho. One of the few diaspora figures press has named.

artists.name: Byu Har (Min Oat Myanmar)
artists.note: SAFETY: INCARCERATED. Described by BBC as one of Myanmar's biggest hip-hop artists; son of songwriter Naing Myanmar. Arrested 24 May 2023 after a Facebook Live criticising power cuts and calling Min Aung Hlaing incompetent, held at North Dagon Police Station, and sentenced to 20 years on 24 Aug 2023. Press reports charge incitement (Penal Code art. 505(a)) and treason, but AP quotes a relative saying it was unclear which he was convicted of - so no single offence is asserted here. Rappler (Mar 2025) documents pro-military Telegram doxing that preceded the arrest. Stage name only; do not add family details beyond published press, and do not attempt to identify him.

artists.name: Kan Kyi
artists.note: Organiser of MOB Party in Chiang Mai (annual from 2022; 4th edition documented 2025) and producer/lead emcee of Triple Edge. Frames MOB Party as building Thai-Burmese artist relations and raising funds for stateless children at risk of displacement. His verifiable record is entirely as organiser and producer; there is no solo artist page. NOT to be merged with the similarly-credited 'KYI' on the Apple Music Triple Edge page, which is unverified as the same person.

artists.name: Triple Edge
artists.note: CONFLICTED / kept deliberately separate from the Chiang Mai crew: a mass single drop on 10-11 Nov 2021 plus a run of releases through 2024, two with Thai-script titles. The Apple Music page carries no location, and the link to the Chiang Mai group is an inference, not sourced. Not merged.

artists.name: Louz Xa Lone
artists.note: Age 24 in Mar 2021 per Coda Story, 'making music for six years', 84,000+ Facebook followers; released 'The Voices' 3 Feb 2021 as a Facebook video. Best-documented post-coup solo act, though identity remains a pseudonym. His 2024 'Naung Kyoe' with PHATKIDz and Reload is confirmed on two independent platforms.

artists.name: Vanzzzo
artists.note: The archive's strongest diaspora datapoint: a Myanmar national who claimed asylum in the US in 2009, aged 22 in Mar 2021, released 'Rebel (Save Myanmar)' in March 2021. Coda Story is the only source and the asylum claim is self-reported. No solo artist page; appears only as a feature on other artists' records.

artists.name: Yung Hugo
artists.note: From the Karen ethnic group; fans called 'Yummies'. SELF-IDENTIFIES AS FOURTH GENERATION: 'The pioneer of Myanmar hip hop is Acid. I'm fourth-generation.' (HipHopDX, Mar 2022). Also: 'for me, 2010 to 2015 were the golden age of hip hop but I was told during these years, there were no shows. I want to rebuild the golden age of hip hop in Myanmar before I am gone.' His 2023 album Make Karen Great Again is a Karen-language record, an ethnic-language marker distinct from the Yangon-centre framing of earlier periods.

artists.name: Adjustor
artists.note: The most documented solo act in the BG18 post-coup circle: five releases 2020-2024 including four full-length projects. CREDIBILITY WARNING: Apple Music's genre field reads 'Pop' for this artist; that is a metadata error and is not recorded as a stylistic claim.

artists.name: GRACEe
artists.note: CONFLICTED: Apple Music hosts 'GRACEe' and 'Grace' as SEPARATE artist entities with overlapping personnel, and AllMusic uses both spellings in one entry. Not merged. LIFTED highlights 'Zat Poh' as a blend of hip pop and R&B over a lo-fi beat.

artists.name: TRIGGER
artists.note: 'DON'T KILL MY VIBE' with 223 on a Jersey Club beat, reviewed by LIFTED in Aug 2023.

artists.name: 13 THREE
artists.note: Part of the four-way drill collaboration 'RUN' (2023) with XMA, CEYYIE and ABET - the clearest documentation of drill entering the Burmese new wave.

artists.name: XMA
artists.note: Part of the four-way drill collaboration 'RUN' (2023).

artists.name: CEYYIE
artists.note: Part of the four-way drill collaboration 'RUN' (2023).

artists.name: ABET
artists.note: Part of the four-way drill collaboration 'RUN' (2023).

artists.name: Arr G
artists.note: LIFTED's scene report notes 'SMD' as unusually animositous even by the new wave's standards.

artists.name: KN
artists.note: 'Eyez On Me' with Reload, an homage to 2Pac's track name.

artists.name: N.A.W
artists.note: Features on Myat Amara Maung's 2025 album Amygdala and on Yan's 2026 Zen Music release.

artists.name: Meemi
artists.note: 'We Got This (Myanmar Song to Fight against Military Dictatorship)', 18 Feb 2021 - a direct anti-coup single in the first weeks after 1 February.

artists.name: Si Thu Aung
artists.note: Graffiti artist who painted coup-protest murals nationwide in early 2021. Included because the archive's scope includes graffiti as a hip-hop element, and RAJ explicitly counts graffiti artists in its alliance.

artists.name: NAY
artists.note: UNRESOLVED IDENTITY WARNING. At least two real-name candidates circulate for NAY in platform credits: Nay Ye Khant (songwriter on Lil Kee Boi's 'Mother Teresa') and Nay Thit Nyein (writer/composer on 99 Symphony and Lil Max releases). NAY also appears to be two roles at once - an artist on feature credits, and the mastering engineer on 223's official videos ('Mastered by Nay'), with a possible third 'Nay' on 'Barback'. These are NOT merged without further evidence. A shared surname with Pyi Bhone Khant makes kinship plausible but unproven.

artists.name: Thar Thar
artists.note: Duet partner of Htet Yan on 'Shae Mhi Nout Mhi' (2018), which contained the #1 hit 'Nway Thwar Tal'. Distinct from Thar Thar the writer/producer associated with X-Boxin.

artists.name: LiL Max
artists.note: Co-billed with 223 on 'MOMMA I'M CRIMINAL' (2026) and on tracks from 223 Da World.

artists.name: I & O
artists.note: Artist billing on Rap Against Junta's Bandcamp single 'Came From Hell' (2022). Membership unknown.

artists.name: BXMB The Tank
artists.note: Frequent Triple Edge collaborator on the 2021-2022 single run.

artists.name: Lil Cado
artists.note: DECEASED, date unknown. Billed as 'Lil Cado (Rip)' on the Myanmar Hip Hop Channel by December 2025. Founding member of 223 (with Yungpunch and Zero) and its mixer. A posthumous 'Lil Cado Song Collection' of 223 re-uploads appeared in Dec 2025. `died` is left null because no source gives a date; `activeTo` records only the latest year he is documented alive. Date and cause of death are not in any source found.

artists.name: Lil'Z
artists.note: Part of Htet Yan's four-album collective; appeared on the FIRST STEP show and on Hlwan Paing's Guitar Lesson.

artists.name: Nine One
artists.note: Appeared on the FIRST STEP show, May 2016.

artists.name: MC Bay Gyi
artists.note: Recorded 'Epic Comeback' with Zay Ye' and Yan Yan in 2023 (Destino Label). Note: 'Ba Gyi' is also credited as a beatmaker in the 2010s underground circuit; whether these are one person is UNRESOLVED.

artists.name: SLO9E
artists.note: Collaborates with blazy on 'Number (N) Ine' and 'One for All'.

artists.name: Doublej
artists.note: In the BG18 circle and the Full Stop live circuit; appears on Reload's 'One Hunnid' (2023) with X-Boxin and #RB2.

artists.name: Naung Naung
artists.note: Named as a 4th-generation cohort act by Coconuts in 2017 and a guest performer at The Showdown freestyle battle.

artists.name: Hein Htet Zaw
artists.note: THREE NAMES, ONE PERSON. 'HOT' and 'OT the Croc' are both this artist - two independent publisher descriptions state the identity (Chartmetric's bio string-concatenates 'This is Hein Htet Zaw (a.k.a) HOT.' with 'OT the croc, born Mandalay', and the Burmese Plug Talk podcast episode description reads 'Ot the croc aka Hein Htet Zaw'). The release titles HOT BLODDED CROC and CROC MOVE (SEASON 1) corroborate the croc motif on the HOT streaming identity. Born Mandalay, grew up on the north side of the city. Rapping from 2013; producing beats from 2016, and described as 'one of the most productive beat producers from Area 952' - Area 952 is UNVERIFIED as to what it denotes. Credited as (WCC) in Jan 2014, so affiliated with that crew by then; 'Studio Mandalay' is credited on the same track. Collaborators he names: Frezzy, A Tee, Datty Dax, L.O.D, BIGG, Weei4, S-Two, Tyrant, Jerryx, JCZ, Bobby Beatz. CAUTION: do not conflate with Hein Htet (rock band Out Of The Rule) or Hein Htet Aung - three distinct Burmese artists. Do NOT record ဦးတိုက် as his script name: ဦး is the honorific 'U', making ဦးတိုက် read as 'U Toik', which is not a plausible mononym and not a transliteration of 'OT'. No source uses it.

artists.name: Wareru
artists.note: Singer-rapper with a substantial 2011-2017 hip-hop catalogue: collaborations with Max Yang, Sean Vidarr, Niffle Yone, Sai Thar Kyaw and J-Me, a 12-track mixtape in 2017, and a Jam It! artist listing. CITY UNVERIFIED - the archive's own earlier note placed him in Mandalay and that is NOT supported; do not assume a city. The commonly repeated 'Shan/Pa-O singer-rapper' framing is also not sourceable: no statement of ethnicity or region was found. CAUTION: a generic search for this name returns the 13th-century Mon king Wareru/Wagaru of the Martaban Kingdom, who is a different person entirely. His 2017 mixtape also appears on Spotify under the same title with a matching track list, which is a suspected re-release rather than a second release.

artists.name: Khaing Myal Kyaw Swar
artists.note: Born and raised in Nan Taw Shae, Mandalay. RAPPER-PRODUCER, later with 360 Beatz for management and distribution. Start year CONFLICTED across two platforms - his own LinkedIn bio says early 2013, Playboard says early 2014; unresolved. His Ultrasonic Record affiliation and the 'Stoner's Book' mixtape rest on that SINGLE self-authored bio: no label page, no release page, no press. Treat as single-source. CAUTION: a Playboard 'about' paragraph praises 'Kyaw Swar 100' with no named critic or outlet; that is promotional boilerplate and is not recorded as a critical reception. Also distinct from Wareru's producer credit 'Kyaw Swar'.

artists.name: A TEE ALL CAPS
artists.note: Self-described Mandalay act on SoundCloud, releases published 2025-12-01: an A-Z numbered track series ('01 A. Cats Don't Submerge Long', '04 O. Eraserhead', '05 U. 0.5 mm Lead Refill', '06 Countess and Her Esquire', '08 I. 1_4 Days of Sodom', '10 Koyaanisqatsi'). The all-caps styling is the artist's own. A Mandalay act called A Tee demonstrably exists in Hein Htet Zaw's circle: his bio names 'A Tee' among his collaborators and the 'SWAMP THING' posse cut credits ATEE. NO SOURCE FOR 'UNOFFICIAL ATEE' in any form - whether that is a label, a mixtape-series subtitle, a crew or an error is UNVERIFIED. Heavy name collision: A-tee also resolves to a South African duo, a London DJ, a Beatport tech-house act, Lyrical A-tee, JustaTee, and ATEEZ.

artists.name: Alatt
artists.note: Wildboy member and Y-Zet's duet partner on 'The Collaboration' (2010). Has his own mixtapes - Urban Revolution (2014), a 2015 mixtape and a 2016 Collector's Edition - and appears on Y-Zet's debut album ဇ. Also mixed the 2012 MRC track 'Beef လုပ်မွာလား'. No real name and no city in any source; Mandalay membership is inferred from Wildboy, which is itself Mandalay-based.

artists.name: Mg Moe Aung
artists.note: Wildboy member. The most frequent voice on the Wildboyz Entertainment Mixtape (2013), appearing on four of its twelve tracks. Collaborated with Y-Zet on 'အေဝးနှင့်ချို (Zaw Gyi)' (2013) and with Oasix on 'My Baby Boo Tax' (2013). Co-made the diss 'Shwee Die' with Y-Zet and Oasix. No real name and no city in any source.

artists.name: Dr.13
artists.note: Wildboy member. Appears on the Wildboyz Entertainment Mixtape (2013) and made 'Scream' with Y-Zet. No real name, city or solo discography in any source.

artists.name: J-Fire (Mandalay)
artists.note: DISTINCT from the Yangon J-Fire already in the archive, which appears on a 2013 Wildboy-adjacent compilation. This one self-describes as 'Burmese Hip-Hop Musician from Mandalay, Myanmar' and 'Est. 2010' on his own site. His album မႏၲေလး တပင္ေရႊထီး appears on the archived fan site. CAUTION: viberate.com publishes fabricated prose and garbled pseudo-transliterated 'song titles' for this artist (e.g. 'lng:lkpkyliu') and was explicitly excluded. Release dates unverified. Kept separate from the Yangon J-Fire because the two have no confirmed connection.

artists.name: Mc Black Saturn
artists.note: Named on the Nov 2012 'Mdy all stars (6 Stars Ratin") compilation with Channel Wildboy, Mg Secondz, Sai Thar Kyaw, MC Min Thant and Mr Dirt Dino. No bio.

artists.name: Sai Thar Kyaw
artists.note: On the Nov 2012 MDY All Stars compilation and on the 2013 'Battle Cry' with Wareru and Sean Viddar. Also a guest performer at the 2018 Yangon Showdown freestyle battle, which is direct evidence of Mandalay-Yangon circuit traffic.

artists.name: Sean Viddar
artists.note: Features on Wareru's 2017 mixtape and the 2013 'Battle Cry' with Wareru and Sai Thar. Also on Y-Zet's ဇ album. Burmese-script spellings in the fan archive are ရွှီးဒိုင်း (Sean Vidarr) and စီယန်ဗစ္စဒတ်ဒတ် (Sean Viddar).

artists.name: Max Yang
artists.note: Features on Wareru's 2017 mixtape ('မွတ္တိုင္') and on the 2011 'Bruce Lee' with Wareru and Niffle Yone.

artists.name: Frezzy
artists.note: Named as a Hein Htet Zaw collaborator and credited on the 11-way 'SWAMP THING' posse cut. Also appears on 99 Symphony's INTERNATION credit list.

artists.name: Channel Wildboy
artists.note: Billed 'Channel Wildboy' on the MDY All Stars track, which independently confirms Wildboy affiliation. Appears on four Wildboyz mixtape tracks and with Oasix, Alatt, TMH and Lout Lout on the posse cut 'Boucher'.

artists.name: Solo
artists.note: Mandalay Rapperz Crew member, credited on the 2011 Mandalay Rapperz Crew Mixtape. No other sourcing.

crews.note: Never released an album; circulated songs plus planned B-Clipz and solo mixtapes. Aung Ye' Htike ran the MMHLS lyric-video channel and credited beats to Ba Gyi and MC Nay. Names recorded in the source but without their own entity record: aung-phyo-mrc, kzt, nga-ye, doe-z, g-miner, soe-shar, yan-naing, ye-myat, naing-ngan, melody, thiha-swe, phyo-thu, ko-hein, tha-hla.
