crews.note: Studio rather than a rap group. Htet Mon signed studio email addresses and recorded with $tringz and Pa South Production. Names recorded in the source but without their own entity record: htet-mon, kk, thu-ta.

crews.name: Wildboy (Wildboyz Entertainment)
crews.status: active c. 2009-2013; disbanded 'in some year' (per Oasix's Wikipedia article)
crews.note: Mandalay's principal underground crew. Released a 12-track Wildboyz Entertainment Mixtape in Feb 2013. The clearest documented underground-to-mainstream pipeline in the archive: Oasix and Y-Zet both came out of it. Names recorded in the source but without their own entity record: mg-moe-aung, alatt, dr-13, channel-wb, oo-fat, lout-lout, mg-hann-saw, thu-rain, sai-nay, alone-wb, mg-pyae-phyo, phyo-wai. FULL ROSTER RECOVERED from two independent fan-archive mirrors (mmhiphopchannel and nelmyolay): Oasix, Y-Zet, Mg Moe Aung, Alatt, Dr.13, Channel, TMH, T-Rain/Thu Rain, Sai Nay, Alone, Mg Hann Saw, Lout Lout, Oo Fat, Phyo Wai, Mg Pyae Phyo, Dudue, Plus, Mg Archi and Aung Moe Heinn. Most have no entity record; their ids here are placeholders pending act-level sourcing, and no solo discography exists for any of them. 'Channel Wildboy' appears on the Nov 2012 MDY All Stars compilation, which independently confirms Wildboy membership for Channel. A Mandalay base is INFERRED from Oasix and Y-Zet, not stated on the mixtape page itself.

crews.name: B-Lord Family (BLF)
crews.note: Operated BLF collections and an unreleased-album tape. Names recorded in the source but without their own entity record: ba-chit, kyaw-swar-sett. Ah Boy's presence is inferred from the 2011 'The Reunion - Rock Star + BLF' joint release, not from a BLF roster.

crews.name: SME (Swag Music Entertainment)
crews.status: founded Dec 2009 by Jimmy Jacobs and Luffie; 200+ shows
crews.note: Names recorded in the source but without their own entity record: luffie.

crews.name: BG18 Record Label
crews.note: The label network behind the 2019-2026 Yangon rap cohort. Roster is reconstructed from release credits and may be incomplete; the BG18 website does not publish a roster. Names recorded in the source but without their own entity record: player-k, shine-bg18.

crews.name: Eagle Element
crews.note: Founded by Lil Kee Boi, who describes himself as CEO; Ah Sar is described as its first early member. Copyright strings vary between keethebalenci/ADAR24, Eagleelement@recordlabel, @Keethebalenci//Eagleelement and YoungCeo.

crews.name: Billionaire Minds Group (BMG)
crews.note: The dominant copyright label across the 2023-2026 new wave. Membership is inferred from (P) copyright strings, not from a published roster. Names recorded in the source but without their own entity record: jan-gyi, lil-l-max, slomm, ye-lay.

crews.name: b4 Records
crews.note: UNVERIFIED - no source could be found for a label of this name, and it may be a garbling of Lil Kee Boi's '##B4KTBC' EP. Platform metadata attributes Wink's CD and bkho bain's work to b4 Records, but no label page, press or corporate record exists. Recorded so the attribution is not lost, and flagged so it is not treated as established. bkho bain's debut album is independently documented on FASTLANE Records.

crews.name: The Boombox Entertainment (Boombox Ent)
crews.status: active from 2021; director U Pyae Soe
crews.note: Released the X-Hibition JOOX original album (2021). Names recorded in the source but without their own entity record: alex-dmora, lanbar, benjamin-sum, iron-zin-mar-myint.

crews.name: Legacy Music Network (Legacy Music Co., Ltd)
crews.status: active from 2011; distributor and digital aggregator
crews.note: One of the few organised distribution routes out of the underground era.

crews.name: 360Beatz
crews.status: Myanmar's first professional music agency; management and digital aggregation
crews.note: Describes representing 'traditional, alternative and underground to trending' artists. No public roster.

crews.name: Jam It!
crews.status: active from late 2012; 20+ gigs by 2015, 40+ acts
crews.note: Yangon's best-documented underground live platform, founded by Eaiddhi and Ye Ngwe Soe. Began as an acoustic gig at Kan Daw Gyi Park; works with Wathann Film Festival, the first Yangon Street Art Festival and MTV World. Cross-genre: punk, metal and hip hop on the same bill. A hip-hop label released its first full-length album in 2015.

crews.name: Ultrasonic record
crews.note: Names recorded in the source but without their own entity record: khaing-myal, louzy, tricky, ozie, rich-t. SINGLE-SOURCE: the Ultrasonic Record affiliation and the 'Stoner's Book' mixtape rest entirely on Khaing Myal Kyaw Swar's self-authored LinkedIn bio. No label page, no release page, no press.

crews.name: M.F.G (Myanmar Future Generations)
crews.status: underground group; 9mm were said to have distributed their sample CDs at a performance
crews.note: Named in the Wikipedia politics section as the reason 9mm's name was banned. Roster unknown.

crews.name: New wave label circle (Billionaire Minds Group + Eagle Element)
crews.status: a copyright-label network rather than a genre scene
crews.note: The 2020s new wave resolves into a tight label network rather than a geographic or crew-based scene. This pseudo-crew exists to record that finding; it has no membership and no releases of its own.

crews.name: Triple Edge (Chiang Mai)
crews.note: A Chiang Mai collective led by Kan Kyi, organiser of MOB Party. Recorded a mass single drop on 10-11 Nov 2021. DVB is the only outlet with a sustained beat on this scene. Membership is inferred from recurring joint billing on the group's 2021-2022 releases; no source publishes a roster, and 'KYI' on the platform credits is NOT established as Kan Kyi.

crews.name: A New Burma
crews.status: exile arts collective; shows in Bangkok, London, Manchester, Melbourne
crews.note: Not rap-specific, but the main Chiang Mai infrastructure for exiled Myanmar artists, and therefore the nearest thing the diaspora has to a scene organiser. Names recorded in the source but without their own entity record: hnin-win.

crews.name: Zen Music
crews.status: credits 2026 releases including 223's 'MOMMA I'M CRIMINAL' and Yan's 'SCG'

crews.name: Solatido Entertainment
crews.status: released '12 Yar Thi' (2018) as a joint Nay & Reload album

crews.name: Myanmar HipHop Association (M.H.A.)
crews.note: Formed unofficially; many youths joined and were inspired to become hip-hop artists. LIFTED's 2023 scene report covers an MHA 'Knockout' release, so the association still functions as a live brand decades after the 2002 wave.

crews.name: Generation Wave
crews.note: A pro-democracy youth network using music, graffiti and pamphlets. Phyo Zeya Thaw was a member and served six years, released 17 May 2011; he was executed on 25 July 2022. Must not be collapsed into any rap crew.

crews.name: VIP (Rock$tar)
crews.status: active; Ah Boy is a former member
crews.note: ONE GROUP, TWO NAMES - not a name collision. A 2009 Myanmar Hip Hop Channel interview has Kyaw Htut Swe stating the group began in 2007 with Ah Boy and Htein Win, that Htein Win is Kyaw Htut Swe's younger brother, and that for various reasons only three stayed long-term, with Jouk Jack added. The 2009 mixtape 'Titans (G-Fam, BNW, Fire-Cracker, Rockstar)' places Rock$tar alongside three OTHER crews, and the collective track 'Revison (Rock Star)' credits all four members. Wikipedia renders the name as 'VIP (Rock$tar)'. Htein Win is not given his own artist record, so the four-member group appears as three member ids. Kyaw Htut Swe also states candidly that the members joined for the sample CDs, not for musical ability. Ah Boy's exit is the documented event: his Wikipedia article lists him as 'Formerly of Rock$tar' and 'former lead vocalist', and a Feb 2013 Burmese headline implies a grievance about him not pulling his weight rather than a rupture. No response from the group is on record.

crews.name: Mandalay Rapperz Crew (MRC)
crews.status: active from 2011; self-labelled 'Crew' on the release
crews.note: MANDALAY, not Yangon - and distinct from the Yangon M.R.C (Nine Win) crew already in the archive, which shares the initials. Corroborated by a member's own contact address ending '.mdy' (the standard Mandalay abbreviation). Members: Ye' Myat, Na Yem, Na Jyam, Nga Ye', Aung Phyo, Kyaw Zin, Yan Naing, Doe-Z, Thiri Yadanar, Su Thet Nge, plus special guest No No. Recorded at studio TKG with lyrics and beats by MRC. NOTE: their 'Mandalay Love & Hate' Vol-1+2 (Sep 2012) is pop/R&B, not rap, and is flagged as such. Names recorded here but without their own entity record: Na Yem, Na Jyam, Nga Ye', Kyaw Zin, Yan Naing, Doe-Z, Thiri Yadanar, Su Thet Nge, No No.

crews.name: Error MDY
crews.note: Mandalay collective - 'mdy' is the standard city abbreviation. Members: Heinz, K-Square, NTZ, M2K, Mc R-K, Hein Min, Phone Myat, Wai Phyo Lin, Ko Peter. Released a 14-track mixtape in Aug 2013 and a Thingyan mixtape in 2015. No member has an entity record, so memberIds is empty and the roster is preserved here.

crews.name: Thar Nge (MC Family)
crews.note: The strongest Mandalay-scene evidence in the fan archive: two of Oasix's and Y-Zet's seven guest appearances on the 2013 mixtape, from the crew they both belonged to at the time. Members and associates: Joe Joe, B-Boi, Khaing Soe, Timmy, Wailin Phyo, Thaw Thaw, and Chan Myae (Mandalay Rapperz Crew). CITY UNVERIFIED - no source states Mandalay, though the crossover with both Wildboy members makes it plausible. CAUTION: at least three distinct Burmese artists are called Thar Nge - this rap crew, the Myanmar Idol S2 winner Thar Nge (b. Zaw Win Htun 1992, pop/R&B), and jazz vocalist Thar Nge IV (b. 1988, Yangon). Never merge. Also distinct from Thar Thar, Htet Yan's duet partner.

crews.name: MDY All Stars (6 Stars Ratin')
crews.note: Various-artists compilation: Mc Black Saturn, Channel Wildboy, Mg Secondz, Sai Thar Kyaw, MC Min Thant and Mr Dirt Dino. Its value is as cross-city evidence - Channel Wildboy independently confirms Wildboy membership, and Sai Thar Kyaw and MC Min Thant both appear at Yangon's 2018 Showdown battle.

crews.name: WCC
crews.note: Crew or affiliation tag on the archived fan site. Hein Htet Zaw is billed 'Hein Htet Zaw(WCC)' on 'Welcome 2 Mandalay' (Jan 2014, studio Studio Mandalay) and Joe Joez is tagged (WCC) too. No roster, no city, no releases. Mandalay inferred from the track's title and studio only.

crews.name: Studio Mandalay
crews.note: Recording studio credited on Hein Htet Zaw's 'Welcome 2 Mandalay' (2014) and on the 2012 'Second Battle' recording with MC Mic, Hein Htet Zaw, Shine Khant and Soe K. One of the few named Mandalay studios in the record.

crews.name: Frenzo
crews.status: a music production company owned by Sai Sai Kham Leng, 2010-2016
crews.note: CORRECTED: Frenzo is not a 'Yangon collective' as the archive previously implied. It is a music production company owned by Sai Sai Kham Leng, and G Fatt, Nay Win, Bunny Phyoe and Phyo Lay were artists signed to it from 2010-2016. Aung Thu is Nay Win's cousin and a Snare member, not central to Frenzo. No dispute involving Frenzo was found in any source searched.

crews.name: b4 Records
crews.note: FLAGGED AS UNVERIFIED. No source for a label called 'b4 Records' could be found in this research pass, and it is possibly a garbling of Lil Kee Boi's '##B4KTBC' EP. bkho bain's debut album BLUE ON BLUE is independently documented on FASTLANE Records, and Wink's CD is attributed to b4 Records in platform metadata - but no corporate, press or platform page for the label itself exists. Recorded so the two artists' platform labels are not lost, and so this can be corrected when a real source appears.

releases.title: Thar Nge (MC Family) Mixtape
releases.note: 2013, 7 tracks: 1 မင္းပညာဒါအကုန္ပဲလား; 2 There For You (ft Oasix); 3 Celebrity အရူး; 4 မနက္ျဖန္အထိ (ft Y-Zet); 5 ငါ့ကိုမုန္းလိုက္ (ft Oasix); 6 ေစာက္တလြဲလုပ္သူမ်ား (ft Y-Zet); 7 အမုန္းရဲ့အစ (Cypher Love). THE STRONGEST MANDALAY-SCENE EVIDENCE IN THE ARCHIVE: two of Oasix's and Y-Zet's seven guest appearances come from a crew they both belonged to at the time. Crew members: Joe Joe, B-Boi, Khaing Soe, Timmy, Wailin Phyo, Thaw Thaw, and Chan Myae of Mandalay Rapperz Crew. City UNVERIFIED - the crossover with Wildboy makes Mandalay plausible but no source states it.

releases.title: Thar Nge Song Collection
releases.note: Mar 2013, 10 tracks featuring Shwe Htoo, Timmy, Joe Joe and B Boi.

releases.title: Mdy all stars (6 Stars Ratin')
releases.note: Nov 2012. Mc Black Saturn, Channel Wildboy, Mg Secondz, Sai Thar Kyaw, MC Min Thant, Mr Dirt Dino. Valuable as cross-city evidence: Channel Wildboy independently confirms Wildboy membership, and Sai Thar Kyaw and MC Min Thant both appear at Yangon's 2018 Showdown battle.

releases.title: တစ္သက္တာမွတ္တိုင္းႏွင့် အေတြးအေခၚမ်ား
releases.note: 2017, 12 tracks, full tracklist: 1 စစ္သည္တေယာက္ရဲ႕သြားရာလမ္း; 2 အေရးေတာ္ပံုက်မ္း; 3 မွတ္တိုင္ (ft Max Yang); 4 ေက်ာ္စြာ (ft Soul Seven); 5 ေအာင္ေဇယ်; 6 အာဠာ၀ကရဲ႕ ညစာ; 7 အျခားပလက္ေဖာင္း; 8 ရဲစိတ္ (ft Sean Viddar); 9 သူ႔ႏွလံုးသားမွ စကားေျပာေသာအခါ; 10 ေရႊမန္းဆီသို႔ (ft Ko Zay); 11 ၂၁ ရာစု လူခၽြန္လူေကာင္း; 12 ခ်စ္ေရးဆို. A Spotify album carries the same title with a matching track list and is a SUSPECTED RE-RELEASE, not a second release.

releases.yearNote: UNVERIFIED: Spotify lists no year and the catalogue sits in a 2026 window. Suspected re-release.

releases.yearNote: UNVERIFIED: no year in any source.
releases.note: Includes 'SWAMP THING', an 11-way collaboration with FREZZY, KAP Y, STWO, BIGG, ATEE and T FLOW - the clearest cross-link between the Hein Htet Zaw circle and A TEE.

releases.note: Aug 2014, 6 tracks: ABCD (ft Yang KG); Dirty Mann (with Joe Joez); Middle Region Evening (with Dattha); Heart Record (New Version); Nout Sone Pal; My Elder. An ONLINE mixtape circulated by download in 2014 - evidence of the pre-streaming distribution era, and named for it.

releases.yearNote: UNVERIFIED: after c.2013, before 2020.
releases.note: With Louzy, Tricky, Ozie and Rich T. SINGLE-SOURCE: rests entirely on the artist's own LinkedIn bio.

releases.title: ONE TAKE
releases.note: Raw one-take recordings plus remixes of three 1990s hip-hop tracks - a self-documented archivist impulse by a Mandalay rapper-producer.

releases.title: Y-Zet ဇ (debut solo album)
releases.note: Released 10 June 2017, 13 tracks plus a bonus. FULL TRACKLIST: 01 ေရဆန္လမ္း; 02 သူရဲေကာင္းတုိ႔မိခင္; 03 သင္းကြဲတိမ္; 04 မ်က္လွည့္ (ft Shwe Htoo); 05 အဆုိေတာ္ၾကီး; 06 Warning (ft Lil' Z); 07 ေကာက္ေတး (ft G-Clock); 08 မျဖစ္သင့္ေသာ; 09 ေခါင္းေတြေမာ့ထား; 10 ျပႆနာ (ft Oasix & Alatt); 11 ဘယ္သူလဲ (ft Shwe Htoo & Oasix); 12 ခရမ္းျပာလိပ္ျပာမ်ား (ft Zarni); bonus 13 မွ အခန္း၄၇. Note this is the album whose promotion six weeks later turned fatal. Wikipedia glosses the title ဇ as 'Gene'; ဇ is the Burmese letter *za*.

songs.title: A Ngweh A That Myar (အငွေ့အသက်များ)
songs.note: With ChanMyae MgCho. Peaked at #1 on the JOOX top 100 and won the JOOX 2020 Popular Song Award - the archive's clearest example of a Burmese rap single crossing into the mainstream market.

songs.title: Generation Driven by Faith
songs.note: Posthumous. Opens with a voice note of Zayar Thaw saying he wrote the bars while serving his prison sentence and never finished them. Released through Rap Against Junta.
With JCZ; the hit that raised his profile before Blessed.

songs.title: Nway Thwar Tal
songs.note: With Thar Thar. #1 hit; went viral on TikTok in early 2019 with 50,000+ user videos and was later sampled in an Imagine Dragons melody, per Coconuts.

songs.title: Yabwar Kalu (My People)
songs.note: A S'gaw Karen-language hit. Part of the ethnic-language rap evidence behind the fourth-generation framing.

songs.title: Waytaku Bwar Kanyaw

songs.title: Thit Sar

songs.title: Eyez On Me

songs.title: Zat Poh

songs.title: SMD

songs.title: Rebel (Save Myanmar)

songs.note: 223 feature with NAY, from 223 Da World. A per-track feature on a lead artist's album, so it resolves the artist through Song rather than through the release's lead credit.

songs.title: Don't Trap
songs.note: With Yan and LiL Max on a 223 Da World track.

songs.title: sin4me
songs.note: With 223 on a 223 Da World track.

songs.note: Lil Kee Boi feature on Ah Sar's debut EP - the clearest correction of the common aggregator error that Prodigy Kid is a Kee Boi release.

songs.title: ဘယ်ညာ

songs.note: With Moe Htet and Nay Ye Khant, from X-Boxin's album 99. One of the few records that bridges the fourth generation and the post-coup scene; note that 'Nay Ye Khant' here may or may not be the same person as 'NAY' - see artists.json.

songs.title: Generation Driven by Faith

events.name: Full Stop's Straight Outta Yangon: Chapter 2
events.note: ACID reunion show; exact date approximate (announced as 'tonight' in Sep 2017 article)

events.name: Sai Sai Birthday Show
events.note: Annual outdoor concert starting 10 April 2004

events.name: Y-Zet album promotion concert (Mandalay)
events.note: Turned violent: one 19-year-old died and the event was shut down. One of the few documented fatal incidents at a Burmese hip-hop event.

events.name: FIRST STEP Hip Hop Music Show
events.note: Myaw Sin Island, Kandawgyi Park, Yangon. A free public-park show - the opposite of the paid hotel circuit, and evidence that the scene still had public access to live performance in 2016.

events.name: Monsoon II (Full Stop)
events.note: Yangon International Hotel, with house DJs flown in from Bangkok. Part of Charlie Artingstoll's Full Stop series.

events.name: Straight Outta Yangon Round 3 (Full Stop)
events.note: Early December 2016, 9pm-4am, at The Clubhouse. Full Stop series; line-up not recorded in the source.

events.name: Straight Outta Yangon: Chapter 2 (ACID reunion, Full Stop lineup)
events.note: The Clubhouse, Kandawgyi Palace Hotel. ACID reunion plus the Full Stop roster. The pre-existing ev-straight-outta-yangon-2 record (dated 15 Sep 2017 from the Coconuts article) is retained separately; the two dates conflict and are NOT merged. Only performers with an existing artist record are listed.

events.name: The Showdown Freestyle Battle
events.note: Urban Asia Center, downtown Yangon, Saturday 8 Sept, 16 freestyle rappers from across Myanmar, judged by Anegga (ACID co-founder). Guest performances by Yan Yan Chan, G-Tone, Bo Htet, Nay, Ba Htoo, Jeep Jeep, Naung Naung, Young Beatz and Min Thant. Sponsored by Grand Royal Signature whiskey. YEAR IS UNVERIFIED - the Coconuts article is undated; do not assume 2018.

events.name: Break the Night
events.note: Myanmar-France-Germany hip-hop project organised by Institut Francais de Birmanie with Goethe-Institut Myanmar. DJ Densen (DE), Saw Phoe Kwar, Tyrah-T, Boby Funk, Chan A Win; hip-hop battle plus an open graffiti wall, free, 6:30-11:30pm. The clearest documented instance of graffiti as part of a hip-hop event.

events.name: Heavy Weight album promotion show (Time City Yangon)
events.note: Promotion for Bo Htet's album whose date is itself CONFLICTED between 2020 and 2023 across platforms.

events.name: MOB Party (3rd annual)
events.note: Parking lot at Cool Muang Coffee near Tha Phae Gate, Chiang Mai. Thai, Myanmar and international participation. Raises funds for children who remain stateless and are at risk due to displacement and lack of access to education. NOTE: the 1st and 2nd editions (2022, 2023) are implied by 'annual' and 'third annual' but no article for them exists, so they are NOT recorded as events.

events.name: MOB Party (4th annual)
events.note: Democrazy!, Chiang Mai. Thai headliner Elevenfinger was released from prison in Thailand shortly before this edition.

events.name: Overflow Music Festival
events.note: Eastern Yangon Event Park. bkho bain (as Thein Min Htike) and Wink (as Ye Wint Aung, 'Bala') performed material using obscene language and distributed condoms. Police arrested participants between 5 and 6 Nov; 16 people were charged under Myanmar Penal Code ss. 505(b) and 294, with arrests in Tamwe, Yankin and Thingangyun townships. One of the clearest documented instances of legal repression of a live hip-hop event.

events.name: Jam It! first show (Kan Daw Gyi Park)
events.note: Began as an acoustic gig, late 2012. Jam It! went on to 20+ gigs by 2015 across Yangon and Mandalay with 40+ acts, cross-genre with punk, hard rock and metal, plus live graffiti artists. The best-documented underground live platform in the archive.

events.name: Rap Against Junta first public show
events.note: A few weeks after the coup, on a sidewalk next to a police station in downtown Yangon: 4-5 performers, 1-2 hours.

events.name: Rap Against Junta second show
events.note: Staged with the cooperation of a large Yangon shopping mall; the power was cut mid-concert.

events.name: DICKCOUNCIL album listening party
events.note: Held on YouTube at 21:15 HKT. An online launch for an album released while the country had no reliable internet - the clearest single illustration of why the international platforms are also the archive.

events.name: X-BOXIN's House Party
events.note: Hard Rock Cafe Yangon, May 2018.

events.name: SCARR - Resilience Arts Exhibition
events.note: Chiang Mai, 27-28 June 2026. 20 Myanmar artists, many living in hiding or on precarious legal status in Thailand; co-organised with Artists' Shelter. SAFETY: participants are deliberately unnamed in the source and one is credited only as 'Harry'. Do not attempt to identify. Recorded as context for the conditions the exile scene works under, not as a hip-hop event.

events.name: 4 Elements residency exhibition (A New Burma)
events.note: Infra Practice Chiang Mai, 21-24 May 2026, Norway-backed. A New Burma, founded by Hnin Win, has worked with 100+ artists since 2022 and has shown in Bangkok, London, Manchester and Melbourne. Not rap-specific, but the nearest thing the diaspora has to scene infrastructure.

events.name: RK Showdown (Mandalay earthquake charity hip-hop show)
events.note: Featuring Myo Kyawt Myaing, Yatha, G-Tone, Jouk Jack and Sandy Myint Lwin. RARE EVIDENCE OF A YANGON-MANDALAY CO-BILL: four of the five performers are Yangon acts appearing in Mandalay, which is the clearest documented instance of cross-city traffic in the archive. G-Tone's presence is notable given his 2007 performance ban.

events.name: Mandalay Rapperz Crew mixtape release
events.note: Recorded at studio TKG. The exact date and venue beyond the studio are not recorded in the source; the venue here is the studio, not a live setting.

events.name: Cover Club Buddha-song DJ set (prosecuted)
events.note: 1-2am. Three DJs played a DJ mix of 'Buddham Saranam Gacchami' and danced in a way reported as disrespecting Buddhism. Charged under s.505(a), case (P)214/2025, Myoma PS; arrested 11 and 13 Sept 2025. Not a rap event - recorded because it is the archive's only documented Mandalay prosecution of a music performer, and because the same s.505(a) architecture catches rappers. Performer names are deliberately not entered as artist records.

events.name: Zayar Thaw sentenced (Lanmadaw Township court)
events.note: Five years under SLORC Law 6/88 (illegal organising) plus one year for foreign currency. Minutes before sentencing he wrote: 'I feel sad, but not because of my imprisonment... I feel sad for the future of our country and people.' Released 17 May 2011.

events.name: Zayar Thaw performance ban, Hmyawzin Island
events.note: Mingala Taungnyunt Township police banned him from performing at a stage show three months after his release from prison. He called it 'doubly punishing'. Recorded because a state that releases a dissident and then bans him from performing is a materially different situation from one that imprisons him.

events.name: G-Tone concert (performance ban)
events.note: G-Tone removed his shirt mid-performance to reveal a tattoo; police handcuffed him as he left the stage but did not detain him, then beat audience members, escalating it into a riot. The Myanmar Music Association banned G-Tone, Thuta and Pyi Tha for one year. CORRECTION to an earlier archive note: this was a BAN, not an arrest, and it happened in 2007. The tattoo's content is disputed between DVB and de Bakker.

sources.title: One dead as brawl breaks out at Y-Zet gig
sources.note: KEY CORRECTION: the 10 June 2017 Mandalay death was NOT a beef killing. The fatal fight began when two groups accidentally elbowed each other while dancing in a packed crowd at a FREE album-promotion concert; four attackers aged 17-20 beat a 19-year-old with a two-foot steel pipe. Eight police and 30 private security were on duty; a friend filed under ss.114 and 302. Six years separate the ~2011 Shwee Die track from the 2017 death. Do not encode a causal relationship.

DO NOT attempt to de-anonymise either. A DIFFERENT article from the swagger-math piece already in sources.

sources.title: DJs, club owner and manager arrested for disrespectful Buddha-song mix in Mandalay
sources.note: 31 July 2025, Cover Club, Mahaaungmye Township, Mandalay. Charged under s.505(a), case (P)214/2025, Myoma PS. Single-source quoting the Myanmar Police Force. Evidence that the legal architecture reaches non-rap music in Mandalay.

sources.title: Artistes held for attempting to disrupt democratic election
sources.note: Law enacted 29 July 2025; arrests from 27-29 Oct 2025 under SAC Law No. 48/2025, penalties 3 years to death. Mostly film and comedy rather than hip-hop, but the same legal architecture that catches rappers.

sources.title: Sham election law and freedom of expression in Myanmar
sources.note: 32 named individuals arrested under the election law by 14 Nov 2025; the junta claimed 88 charged by 29 Oct; Reuters reported at least 229 by Dec 2025. Figures diverge by counting method.

sources.title: Myanmar arrests hundreds under new election law ahead of December vote
In-depth: Myanmar pro-military Telegram channels are doxxing critics
sources.note: CORRECTION: the archive's earlier note dated this March 2025. The investigation is 22 Aug 2023 and the arrest was 24 May 2023. Documents 32 arrests in Jan-May 2023 from Ka Ka Han posts alone, and a FOEIM school data leak of hundreds of students' details. SAFETY: this is the documented mechanism behind Byu Har's arrest - do not publish specific channel handles or personal details.

sources.title: Byu Har (Writer at Risk)
Myanmar hip hop rapper jailed after criticism of power outages
sources.note: AP quotes a relative who spoke anonymously for fear of arrest, and says it was unclear which charge he was convicted of. Do not state a specific offence.

sources.title: Rapper Byu Har arrested over Facebook broadcast
sources.note: Documents the sequence: a 4-minute Facebook video on 23 May 2023 criticising loadshedding in which he gave his home address and invited arrest; calls for his arrest circulating on pro-military Telegram the same day; the night-of arrest by soldiers and police.

sources.title: Myanmar rapper Byu Har arrested over social media rant about erratic power supply
A widespread worry about Myanmar rapper's fate after arrest
Hip hop showdown coming to Mandalay at RK event
sources.note: Earthquake-charity hip-hop show at RK Bar & Music Theatre, Chanmyathazi Township, Mandalay, featuring Myo Kyawt Myaing, Yatha, G-Tone, Jouk Jack and Sandy Myint Lwin - rare evidence of a Yangon-Mandalay co-bill.

sources.title: Bobby Soxer (singer)
sources.note: Documents the 2022 relationship dispute with Hlwan Paing and the veiled diss 'Amyi Tat Pe Pyaw Paing Kwint Mashi'. SAFETY: the song deliberately does not name its target; do not extend allegations to a third party.

sources.title: Artistic creation without naming names
sources.note: Burmese outlet behind the Bobby Soxer diss reporting. Single-sourced; the affair admission is not independently verified.

sources.title: Burmese rapper banned from performing
sources.note: CORRECTION: this was a one-year ban by the Myanmar Music Association, NOT an arrest. G-Tone was handcuffed after leaving the stage but not detained; police then beat audience members, escalating it into a riot. SAFETY: the tattoo's content is DISPUTED - DVB says a back tattoo of clasped praying hands, while de Bakker quoting Yan Yan Chan says rosary beads on a wrist. Coconuts (2015) separately garbles this as a 2008 arrest, wrong on both year and sanction.

sources.title: The Beat of Yangon
sources.author: Jeroen de Bakker
sources.note: Key reporting on the 2007-08 scene: artists slandered, banned and arrested on stage for their lyrics; Acid's Beginning had 16 tracks of which the censor board passed 11; the copy-track economy; and underground-vs-mainstream self-policing.

sources.title: Will copyright problems be solved? (Myanmar film and song copy rights)
sources.note: The most important structural frame for this archive: Thar Si Thaw of the Myanmar Music Association testifies that existing law 'cannot give the necessary protection', so a credit dispute here is usually not a quarrel between artists but an absent legal category.

sources.title: Mock stars: Myanmar's pop plagiarists
sources.note: Documents the 'copy thachin' (copy song) genre as a product of the state's cultural quarantine, including Lay Phyu's Metallica rewrite known domestically as 'Exits'.

sources.title: Rap Against Junta: A Propaganda War Machine for Freedom (Ko Aye Win on the battle form)
sources.author: Shwe Lan Ga Lay
sources.note: The cleanest documented beef analogue in the archive: DICKCOUNCIL producer Ko Aye Win explains deliberately turning the battle form away from other rappers and onto the junta. The host frames it as repurposing an adversarial form against a target not used to being spoken to that way.

sources.title: Y-Zet (full article with discography)
sources.note: The fuller Y-Zet record. Known errors in it: birthplace is Pyin Oo Lwin (Mandalay Region), not Mandalay city; the infobox reads 'Member of: Oasix' on a solo artist; the Burmese letter za is glossed as 'Gene'; and the 'Shwee Die beefing' wording rests on a single now-dead Burmese source whose word choice conflicts with a Korean mirror.

sources.title: SAC issues warrants under s.505(a) for 20 individuals including G Fatt
sources.note: Primary-adjacent: publishes the State Administration Council announcement. Also the source for a separate 2 April list of ~20 more names under s.505(a).

sources.title: Phyo Zeya Thaw
sources.note: Documents the March 2008 arrest, the November 2008 sentence under SLORC Law 6/88 plus a foreign-currency charge, the 17 May 2011 release, his own pre-sentencing and post-release statements, and the August 2011 performance ban. See also the Daily Beast's anonymous-sourced resistance-role claim, recorded separately in disputes.json as unresolved.

disputes.claim: 'Shwee Die' (ရွှီးဒိုင်း, 'flying firecracker') was made by Y-Zet with Wildboy members Oasix and Mg Moe Aung, and is described as dissing Hlwan Paing's song 'Done Pyan' (Rocket).
disputes.response: None recorded. Hlwan Paing has no published reply in any source found.
disputes.evidence: The track's existence is plausible and consistent - all three artists and both target tracks are documented - but the ONLY narrative framing found is one sentence on Wikipedia, citing a single Burmese article (Kumudra, 21 May 2019) that is now unreachable and has no Wayback capture. A Korean-language mirror of the same sentence renders the verb as 'strengthened' rather than 'beefed', which suggests 'beefing' may itself be an editor's interpolation.
disputes.corroboration: single-source, and the primary is dead. No lyrics, no press coverage, no second account.
disputes.corroboratingDetail: Separately, the fan archive shows ရွှီးဒိုင်း was already contested in the underground: a diss track aimed at it, အဆင့္ ('A Sint') by Devil Y & Thar Latt (Y.S.R), appears in the 2012 archive. That is a diss OF the track, which is a different dispute from the track being a diss.
disputes.safety: none known

disputes.claim: A diss track titled အဆင့္ ('A Sint') was made in response to ရွှီးဒိုင်း, i.e. against 'Shwee Die' itself. The archived post title reads 'A Sint For Fucking Shwee Die'.
disputes.response: none recorded
disputes.evidence: The archived post exists in the fan archive with a Burmese subtitle marking it as a response track. The parties credited on it are Devil Y and Thar Latt (Y.S.R).
disputes.corroboration: fan archive only; no press or second account.
disputes.corroboratingDetail: Worth keeping as its own dispute: it shows 'Shwee Die' was a contested object within the underground, not just a diss aimed outward.
disputes.safety: none known

thirdPartiesNamed: an unnamed actress, reported in press
disputes.claim: Bobby Soxer (Htet Htet Aung, b. 22 May 1993) and Hlwan Paing were in a relationship from 2009. She declared on Facebook at the end of 2022 that it had ended, stating the cause was Hlwan Paing's involvement with an actress. Wikipedia summarises this as having 'sparked intense online backlash, prompting Hlwan Paing to later admit to the affair'. She responded with the song 'Amyi Tat Pe Pyaw Paing Kwint Mashi' (နာမည်တပ်ပြီးပြောပိုင့်ခွင့်မရှိ - 'No Right to Speak Without Naming Names'), which indirectly blamed the actress.
disputes.response: Hlwan Paing is reported to have admitted the affair. The actress has no recorded response. Note the song's own title is a claim of indirectness - she denied naming names, so reading it as a direct diss is inference.
disputes.evidence: Wikipedia (Bobby Soxer) citing a Burmese outlet, NP News, 'အနုပညာဖန်တီးမှု အမည်တပ် လိင်အသားပေး ဖျော်ဖြေမှုများ' ('Artistic creation without naming names / singing obliquely'). The earlier relationship is documented by Shwe Mom, 2017.
disputes.corroboration: Wikipedia plus one Burmese outlet. The affair admission is SINGLE-SOURCED and not independently verified. The widely syndicated biography pages all appear to derive from Wikipedia rather than independent reporting.
disputes.corroboratingDetail: This is the clearest documented case in the archive of the scene's actual dispute mechanism: a veiled, deniable diss whose title announces its own indirectness. Combined with the absent copyright law and invisible lyricists, it suggests this scene resolves credit and personal conflicts through the song, not through a lawsuit or a public statement.
disputes.safety: The third party is a living person who is NOT named in the song and must not be named here. Do not extend allegations to her.

disputes.claim: Ah Boy is listed as 'Formerly of Rock$tar' and 'former lead vocalist' of the group. Two Burmese headlines document that his absence was noticed: Yatanarpon News, 'the Rock Star group has been keeping an eye on Ah boy for a long time' (a now-dead link), and a Feb 2013 Myanmar Hip Hop Channel headline roughly meaning 'Ah boy, who has flourished in connection with his not-fulfilling-his-duty'. The second phrasing implies a grievance about him not pulling his weight, not a dramatic rupture.
disputes.response: None recorded. He continued solo and, by 2020, had a #1 JOOX hit.
disputes.evidence: Group composition is well corroborated: a 2009 Myanmar Hip Hop Channel interview has Kyaw Htut Swe stating the group began in 2007 with Ah Boy and Htein Win, that Htein Win is his younger brother, and that Jouk Jack was added; the collective track 'Revison (Rock Star)' credits all four members; and Wikipedia renders the name 'VIP (Rock$tar)'. Kyaw Htut Swe also states candidly that the members joined for the sample CDs rather than for musical ability.
disputes.corroboration: Moderate for the facts, weak for the grievance. The departure is well evidenced; the reason rests on two headlines, one dead, and reading a grievance into Burmese phrasing about a departing member is interpretive.
disputes.corroboratingDetail: The archive previously carried a SEPARATE 'Rock$tar' crew alongside a 'VIP' group, treating the shared name as a collision. It is not: they are one group with two names, and Ah Boy's departure is the real event.
disputes.safety: low
disputes.statusNote: departure settled, reason unresolved

disputes.claim: At a hip-hop concert, G-Tone removed his shirt mid-performance to reveal a tattoo. Police officials handcuffed him as soon as he left the stage - reportedly having been persuaded by other musicians to let him finish his set. He was NOT taken into custody, but the police action 'provoked an angry reaction from the crowd'; police then beat audience members, escalating the incident into a riot. Hip-hop star Yatha intervened and was warned not to get involved again. The Myanmar Music Association banned G-Tone, Thuta and Pyi Tha from performing for one year.
disputes.response: None recorded. G-Tone remains active; he appears on the MHA 'Knockout' posse cut of March 2025.
disputes.evidence: Democratic Voice of Burma, 22 Nov 2007, reporting by Aye Nai. Sanction: a one-year ban by the Music Association.
disputes.corroboration: Single-source (DVB) for the incident. The Independent (2013) and de Bakker independently confirm that Myanmar rappers were targeted over tattoos, but with a DIFFERENT description: de Bakker, quoting Yan Yan Chan, describes 'a bald guy wearing Christian rosary beads on his wrist, but he looked sort of like a monk'. The two accounts of the tattoo do not match.
disputes.corroboratingDetail: CORRECTION to an earlier archive note: this was a BAN, not an arrest, and it happened in 2007 not 2008. Coconuts (2015) separately garbles it as 'in 2008, a Burmese rapper was arrested for the crime of having a tattoo supporting the Saffron Revolution' - wrong on both year and sanction. Wikipedia's 'G-Tone from Cyclone called to question during performing in concert' appears to derive from the same retellings.
disputes.safety: low (historical). G-Tone is alive and active.
disputes.targetDescription: the Myanmar Music Association and the police
disputes.statusNote: ban settled; the tattoo's content is disputed between sources

disputes.claim: Wikipedia's Burmese hip-hop article gives TWO DIFFERENT REASONS in two sentences for the same ban: (i) 'because of the group's alleged political activism, even the name 9mm was banned by the censor board'; and (ii) 'The name 9mm is banned from use in public because they distributed sample CDs of underground group MFG in one of their performance.'
disputes.response: none found
disputes.evidence: Single-source: one Wikipedia footnote, itself [7]. Every downstream mirror (owiki, wiki2.org) reproduces the same text.
disputes.corroboration: None. No primary or press source located. The two stated reasons are mutually inconsistent.
disputes.safety: low (historical, group long inactive)
disputes.statusNote: unresolved. The existence of a ban is asserted only by Wikipedia; the reason is internally contradictory and is recorded here as two competing claims rather than a fact.

disputes.claim: English pro-democracy papers widely reported Yan Yan Chan's April 2008 arrest as democracy-related. Wikipedia's Acid article states that 'the military junta claims that he was actually arrested on drug charges', flagged [citation needed] in the source itself. He was released without charges on 7 January 2009.
disputes.response: No response on record.
disputes.evidence: Wikipedia's Acid article, with the competing junta claim explicitly uncited. Wikipedia's main article adds a [when?] tag to the release date.
disputes.corroboration: The arrest and release are documented. The REASON is two incompatible claims, neither independently established.
disputes.corroboratingDetail: Recorded because this is the only place in the archive where two state and opposition accounts of the same arrest are both live and irreconcilable. Neither is adopted here.
disputes.safety: low (historical). Yan Yan Chan is alive; the disputed drug-charge claim is a serious allegation from an unprovenanced state source and should not be repeated as fact.

disputes.claim: On 23 May 2023 Byu Har posted a four-minute Facebook video from his home in Yangon's North Dagon Township criticising four-hours-on/four-hours-off loadshedding, calling the electricity minister 'a fool' and Min Aung Hlaing 'a stupid incompetent fool', comparing the junta period unfavourably to Aung San Suu Kyi's, and stating his home address in the caption, inviting arrest. Arrested by soldiers and police that night; held at North Dagon Police Station, then Insein. Charged under Penal Code s.505(a); the junta's statement cited incitement to disrupt peace and stability and spreading propaganda. Sentenced to 20 years on 23 August 2023 - reported as the harshest celebrity sentence of the crackdown.
disputes.response: Byu Har made no public response after arrest. The junta's framing is the response on record.
disputes.evidence: Documented sequence, from independent sources: calls for his arrest circulated on pro-military Telegram channels on 23 May; the channel Ka Ka Han (created Oct 2022) described him as 'a low-class dog who swears because there is a blackout in Yangon'; arrest photos were posted to junta Telegram channels on 24 May.
disputes.corroboration: STRONG - five or more independent outlets: AP, BBC, RFA, Mizzima, The Irrawaddy, Bangkok Post, VOA, PEN America, plus Rappler's investigation of the doxing infrastructure. Rappler documents 32 arrests in Jan-May 2023 from Ka Ka Han posts alone, and a FOEIM school data leak exposing hundreds of students' details.
disputes.corroboratingDetail: CORRECTION: the archive's earlier note dated the Rappler investigation to March 2025. It is 22 August 2023, and the arrest was May 2023. The doxing posts are dated the same day as the video, not as a preceding campaign. AP quotes a family member and says it was unclear which charge he was convicted of, so no single offence is asserted here.
disputes.safety: SEVERE. Living prisoner, 20-year sentence. Do not publish his home address, family details, or the specific Telegram channel handles - the doxing mechanism is the documented cause of the arrest. UN Special Rapporteurs called out Telegram's moderation failure in Myanmar in March 2023.
disputes.statusNote: settled as to arrest and sentence

disputes.claim: At the Overflow Music Festival, Eastern Yangon Event Park, Thingangyun Township, a group led by Wink (Ye Wint Aung, aka Bala) and bkho bain (Thein Min Htike) performed twelve songs including '5.55566'. During that song they used obscene language causing public alarm and scattered condoms into the audience, with thirteen people on stage. Police arrested participants between 3 and 6 November; sixteen people were charged.
disputes.response: No artist response on record. Authorities said legal action would proceed 'to ensure appropriate punishment'.
disputes.evidence: CHARGE SECTION CONFLICT: the Myanmar Police Force statement (via Positive Angle News, 8 Nov 2025) gives case file (P)213/2025, Thuwunna PS, sections 505-A, 294 and 114. Eleven Media Group (9 Nov 2025) reports '505(b) and 294'. The primary police statement says 505-A, so that is used here. Separately, DVB names a different performer, Yul Nay Lwin, in the same 'condoms on stage' story - the two namings are NOT merged.
disputes.corroboration: Independent Burmese and English-language outlets agree on the facts and diverge only on the section number.
disputes.safety: HIGH. Named individuals under active prosecution.
disputes.statusNote: unresolved - charges open, no verdict found. Note the NDSC granted amnesty to 724 prisoners serving 505-A sentences on 26 Nov 2025; whether these sixteen fall in that cohort is UNVERIFIED.

disputes.claim: On 3 April 2021 the SAC announced warrants under Penal Code s.505(a) for twenty individuals including G Fatt, accused of encouraging participation in the Civil Disobedience Movement, supporting the CRPH, and inciting disturbance. DVB published the list on 4 April 2021.
disputes.response: None recorded in the sources reached.
disputes.evidence: Primary: the SAC announcement, published by DVB. A second SAC/MRTV list of around twenty more names under s.505(a) followed on 2 April.
disputes.corroboration: Primary for the warrant itself.
disputes.corroboratingDetail: SEPARATE AND UNRESOLVED: G Fatt was publicly criticised after appearing at the military-held Thingyan festival in Naypyidaw on 13 April 2023. This rests on a single source, Mizzima's Spring Revolution Daily News, a resistance-linked daily; the live page could not be fetched and there is no independent confirmation that the criticism was directed at G Fatt rather than another festival performer. Recorded as unresolved rather than as fact.
disputes.safety: HIGH. G Fatt was a s.505(a) warrant subject in 2021 and a target of public denunciation in 2023. The April 2023 Thingyan period is a documented high-risk window for the whole scene.
disputes.statusNote: settled as to the warrant

disputes.claim: At a FREE album-promotion concert for his album ဇ in Mandalay, with thousands attending, mostly teenagers, multiple fights broke out. A group of four beat a 19-year-old with a two-foot steel pipe after an incidental elbowing on the dance floor. The victim died of head injuries at Mandalay General Hospital. Four attackers aged 17-20 were arrested on site. Eight police and 30 private security (MMC Security) were on duty. A friend filed under ss.114 and 302. The event was shut down.
disputes.response: Y-Zet's own on-record apology, in a Burmese interview of 29 March 2018: he said he did nothing wrong but a young man died, and that he accepts his share of the responsibility.
disputes.evidence: Coconuts Yangon, 12 June 2017; The Irrawaddy (Burmese), 12 June 2017, reporting the arrests; 7Day News, 13 June 2017 (cited via Wayback).
disputes.corroboration: STRONG - three independent accounts including two Burmese-language outlets.
disputes.corroboratingDetail: IMPORTANT CORRECTION: this is NOT a beef killing and must never be linked causally to the 2011 'Shwee Die' diss. The fight began with accidental physical contact while dancing, six years after the track. Wikipedia places the two facts in adjacent sections with no causal link, and the earlier archive note that juxtaposed them has been corrected.
disputes.safety: Record only the published facts. The victim is not named in any source and should not be identified beyond 'a 19-year-old'.

disputes.claim: Arrested 12 March 2008 at a restaurant in Yangon with five friends. Sentenced 20 November 2008 by the Lanmadaw Township court to five years under SLORC Law 6/88 (illegal organising) plus one year for foreign currency - his lawyer stated the currency total was under 10,000 kyat. Transferred to Kawthaung prison. Amnesty International named him a prisoner of conscience. Released 17 May 2011. Minutes before sentencing he wrote: 'I feel sad, but not because of my imprisonment... I feel sad for the future of our country and people... Have the courage to reject the things you don't like.'
disputes.response: His own statements, quoted above. Post-release he said: 'While I was in prison, I reconsidered some of my past actions and I felt very uneasy... I don't feel that I've used my full capabilities to help the country.' In August 2011 police in Mingala Taungnyunt Township banned him from performing at a show on Hmyawzin Island, which he called 'doubly punishing'.
disputes.evidence: Mizzima, Amnesty International, The Irrawaddy, BBC, moemaka (an interview with Khet Mar), multiple.
disputes.corroboration: very strong
disputes.corroboratingDetail: Continued repression after release is part of the record, and matters: a state that releases a dissident and then bans him from performing is a different situation from one that imprisons him.
disputes.safety: Deceased by state execution 25 July 2022. Widow and surviving Acid members are at risk and Acid is under surveillance. Do not name safe houses, family, or current members' locations.
disputes.statusNote: settled as to imprisonment and release

disputes.claim: Rearrested November 2021, charged under the Counterterrorism Law and the Public Property Protection Act, sentenced to death January 2022, and executed 23 July 2022 with Ko Jimmy (Kyaw Min Yu) and two others. The Daily Beast reported, citing four anonymous sources with knowledge of the Yangan underground, that he was top commander of the armed resistance in Yangon.
disputes.response: The resistance movement never publicly acknowledged the claim.
disputes.evidence: The arrest, charge, sentence and execution are documented by NYT, AP, BBC, Mizzima, The Irrawaddy, DVB and others. The resistance-role claim rests on four anonymous sources and has never been publicly confirmed by the movement.
disputes.corroboration: very strong for the execution; the resistance role is anonymous-sourced and unconfirmed.
disputes.corroboratingDetail: Recorded because it is exactly the kind of claim an archive should carry WITH its uncertainty attached. Anonymous sourcing from a conflict zone is not the same as a refuted claim, and it is not the same as a verified one either.
disputes.safety: MAXIMUM. Deceased by state execution. Do not name safe houses or family. Note the Observer's evidence that Telenor data located his safe house.
disputes.statusNote: execution settled; resistance role unresolved and contested in character

disputes.claim: DICKCOUNCIL producer Ko Aye Win, a former B-boy who used to battle frequently, told Insight Myanmar: 'Before the coup I was a B-Boy, I liked to battle a lot. But not anymore... Hip hop rap battles, they always like to provoke each other and talk to each other. So I thought, how about we switch the arrow direction in Dickcouncil, to take on the military junta and Min Aung Hlaing or whoever, like every tyrant across the globe!' The interview host frames it as repurposing an adversarial battle form against a target not accustomed to being spoken to that way. DICKCOUNCIL is described as achieving an unprecedented dynamic of Burmese youth openly dissing Min Aung Hlaing.
disputes.response: The junta's response is the broader crackdown, documented elsewhere in this archive.
disputes.evidence: Extended interview with Ko Aye Win by Shwe Lan Ga Lay, Insight Myanmar, 26 December 2021, published on the blog and as a podcast episode.
disputes.corroboration: STRONG - a named, on-record producer explaining the intent in his own words.
disputes.corroboratingDetail: THE CLEANEST BEEF ANALOGUE IN THE ARCHIVE. Almost every other 'beef' here is a genre label, a veiled personal diss, or a censorship record. This one is a dispute in battle form, aimed at the state, with a named participant explaining the pivot on the record. It is also the pivot point of the whole dataset: the target of the adversarial form migrated from other rappers to the regime.
disputes.safety: Do not characterise any platform as safe. Telegram carried the music and was also the doxing channel that led to arrests.
disputes.targetDescription: the Myanmar military government and Min Aung Hlaing
disputes.statusNote: settled as a statement of intent

disputes.claim: At Cover Club, 36th Street and 36x53 Street, Yemon South Ward, Mahaaungmye Township, MANDALAY, from 1-2am on 31 July 2025, three DJs - reported as intoxicated and in indecent clothing - played 'Buddham Saranam Gacchami' as a DJ mix and danced in a way that 'disrespected Buddhism, with the intent to cause outrage towards the Buddhist religion'. Charged under s.505(a), case (P)214/2025, No. (9) Myoma Police Station. Arrested 11 and 13 September 2025; reported 14 September 2025.
disputes.response: None recorded.
disputes.evidence: Eleven Media Group, quoting the Myanmar Police Force.
disputes.corroboration: single-source
disputes.corroboratingDetail: Included despite not being hip-hop, because it is a Mandalay case and because it shows the legal architecture reaching DJs for a religious-desecration charge - the same s.505(a) used against rappers. It is the archive's only documented Mandalay prosecution of a music performer.
disputes.safety: Named individuals under prosecution. One is 24 and reported with a ka title and a name.
partyNames: DJ manager Phyo Hein Ko Ko (Min Htike, 28)

disputes.claim: SAC Law No. 48/2025, the Law on the Prevention of Obstruction, Disruption and Sabotage of Multiparty Democratic General Election, was enacted 29 July 2025 with penalties from three years to the death penalty. From 27 October 2025 artists, actors, comedians and directors were arrested for supporting social-media criticism of the state election-awareness film 'Khit Thamine Ko Done Saing Myi Thu Myar'. Khit Thit Media and other outlets were charged as organisations.
disputes.response: The state framing, per Global New Light of Myanmar.
disputes.evidence: GNLM, the law text and the arrest notices; Myanmar Internet Project's running tally; Reuters.
disputes.corroboration: STRONG, but the totals diverge by counting method: Myanmar Internet Project documented 32 named individuals by 14 Nov 2025; the junta claimed 88 charged by 29 Oct 2025; Reuters reported at least 229 by Dec 2025.
disputes.corroboratingDetail: Mostly film and comedy rather than hip-hop, but it is the same s.505-A plus election-law architecture that catches rappers, and it establishes that by 2025 the legal environment had widened well beyond performance. No artist with a record in this dataset has been charged under it.
disputes.safety: high. No hip-hop artist in this dataset is named as charged.
disputes.statusNote: settled as to the arrests; totals unresolved

disputes.claim: STRUCTURAL, NOT INTERPERSONAL. Thar Si Thaw, a famous singer then head of internal affairs at the Myanmar Music Association, testified to VOA in Burmese on 5 October 2016: 'the existing laws cannot give the necessary protection'. He said he was waiting for the government to fulfil its promise to draft a new copyright law and had been writing and revising the draft himself. He cited enforcement against film and song piracy as the immediate crisis, the music industry resisting, and s.32(a)/(c) as the tools police use. A ministry editorial adviser, Maung Shey, said the ministry was 'personally writing' the law. Separately, the state's cultural quarantine created the 'copy thachin' (copy song) genre - foreign hits rewritten into Burmese - with Lay Phyu's Metallica rewrite of 'Enter Sandman' known domestically as 'Exits'.
disputes.response: The state, via the ministry, was drafting a law as of 2016. Whether it was enacted is UNVERIFIED.
disputes.evidence: VOA Burmese, 5 Oct 2016; The World/PRX on copy-track culture; NBC News/AP; The Independent; de Bakker; J.M. Ferguson in Asia Pacific Journal of Anthropology.
disputes.corroboration: STRONG
disputes.corroboratingDetail: THE MOST IMPORTANT FRAME IN THE ARCHIVE. In this scene a credit dispute is usually not a quarrel between artists but an absent legal category. Phyo Layy writes invisibly as a lyricist for Sandi Myint Lwin, Wine Su Khaing Thein and Warso Moe Oo with no public credit and no documented grievance. A specific investigation of credit disputes involving 99 Symphony's INTERNATION and Phyo Layy found NO dispute exists: Phyo Layy does not appear in that album's writer credits at all. Recorded here so the null result is documented rather than mistaken for an oversight.
disputes.safety: low
disputes.targetDescription: the Myanmar state and the Myanmar Music Association

nodes.label: Aung Ye' Htike
nodes.subtitle: solo
aliases: ေအာင္ရဲထိုက္

nodes.label: M.R.C (Nine Win)
nodes.subtitle: active by 2011-2013; operated MRC Music Production

A Korean-language mirror of the same sentence renders the verb as 'strengthened' rather than 'beefed', which suggests 'beefing' may itself be an editor's interpolation.
disputes.corroboration: single-source, and the primary is dead. No lyrics, no press coverage, no second account.

That is a diss OF the track, which is a different dispute from the track being a diss.

disputes.claim: Bobby Soxer (Htet Htet Aung, b. 22 May 1993) and Hlwan Paing were in a relationship from 2009. She declared on Facebook at the end of 2022 that it had ended, stating the cause was Hlwan Paing's involvement with an actress. Wikipedia summarises this as having 'sparked intense online backlash, prompting Hlwan Paing to later admit to the affair'. She responded with the song 'Amyi Tat Pe Pyaw Paing Kwint Mashi' (နာမည်တပ်ပြီးပြောပိုင့်ခွင့်မရှိ - 'No Right to Speak Without Naming Names'), which indirectly blamed the actress.
disputes.response: Hlwan Paing is reported to have admitted the affair. The actress has no recorded response. Note the song's own title is a claim of indirectness - she denied naming names, so reading it as a direct diss is inference.
disputes.evidence: Wikipedia (Bobby Soxer) citing a Burmese outlet, NP News, 'အနုပညာဖန်တီးမှု အမည်တပ် လိင်အသားပေး ဖျော်ဖြေမှုများ' ('Artistic creation without naming names / singing obliquely'). The earlier relationship is documented by Shwe Mom, 2017.
disputes.corroboration: Wikipedia plus one Burmese outlet. The affair admission is SINGLE-SOURCED and not independently verified. The widely syndicated biography pages all appear to derive from Wikipedia rather than independent reporting.
disputes.corroboratingDetail: This is the clearest documented case in the archive of the scene's actual dispute mechanism: a veiled, deniable diss whose title announces its own indirectness. Combined with the absent copyright law and invisible lyricists, it suggests this scene resolves credit and personal conflicts through the song, not through a lawsuit or a public statement.
disputes.safety: The third party is a living person who is NOT named in the song and must not be named here. Do not extend allegations to her.

disputes.claim: Ah Boy is listed as 'Formerly of Rock$tar' and 'former lead vocalist' of the group. Two Burmese headlines document that his absence was noticed: Yatanarpon News, 'the Rock Star group has been keeping an eye on Ah boy for a long time' (a now-dead link), and a Feb 2013 Myanmar Hip Hop Channel headline roughly meaning 'Ah boy, who has flourished in connection with his not-fulfilling-his-duty'. The second phrasing implies a grievance about him not pulling his weight, not a dramatic rupture.
disputes.response: None recorded. He continued solo and, by 2020, had a #1 JOOX hit.
disputes.evidence: Group composition is well corroborated: a 2009 Myanmar Hip Hop Channel interview has Kyaw Htut Swe stating the group began in 2007 with Ah Boy and Htein Win, that Htein Win is his younger brother, and that Jouk Jack was added; the collective track 'Revison (Rock Star)' credits all four members; and Wikipedia renders the name 'VIP (Rock$tar)'. Kyaw Htut Swe also states candidly that the members joined for the sample CDs rather than for musical ability.
disputes.corroboration: Moderate for the facts, weak for the grievance. The departure is well evidenced; the reason rests on two headlines, one dead, and reading a grievance into Burmese phrasing about a departing member is interpretive.
disputes.corroboratingDetail: The archive previously carried a SEPARATE 'Rock$tar' crew alongside a 'VIP' group, treating the shared name as a collision. It is not: they are one group with two names, and Ah Boy's departure is the real event.
disputes.safety: low

disputes.claim: At a hip-hop concert, G-Tone removed his shirt mid-performance to reveal a tattoo. Police officials handcuffed him as soon as he left the stage - reportedly having been persuaded by other musicians to let him finish his set. He was NOT taken into custody, but the police action 'provoked an angry reaction from the crowd'; police then beat audience members, escalating the incident into a riot. Hip-hop star Yatha intervened and was warned not to get involved again. The Myanmar Music Association banned G-Tone, Thuta and Pyi Tha from performing for one year.
disputes.response: None recorded. G-Tone remains active; he appears on the MHA 'Knockout' posse cut of March 2025.
disputes.evidence: Democratic Voice of Burma, 22 Nov 2007, reporting by Aye Nai. Sanction: a one-year ban by the Music Association.
disputes.corroboration: Single-source (DVB) for the incident. The Independent (2013) and de Bakker independently confirm that Myanmar rappers were targeted over tattoos, but with a DIFFERENT description: de Bakker, quoting Yan Yan Chan, describes 'a bald guy wearing Christian rosary beads on his wrist, but he looked sort of like a monk'. The two accounts of the tattoo do not match.
disputes.corroboratingDetail: CORRECTION to an earlier archive note: this was a BAN, not an arrest, and it happened in 2007 not 2008. Coconuts (2015) separately garbles it as 'in 2008, a Burmese rapper was arrested for the crime of having a tattoo supporting the Saffron Revolution' - wrong on both year and sanction. Wikipedia's 'G-Tone from Cyclone called to question during performing in concert' appears to derive from the same retellings.
disputes.safety: low (historical). G-Tone is alive and active.

disputes.claim: On 23 May 2023 Byu Har posted a four-minute Facebook video from his home in Yangon's North Dagon Township criticising four-hours-on/four-hours-off loadshedding, calling the electricity minister 'a fool' and Min Aung Hlaing 'a stupid incompetent fool', comparing the junta period unfavourably to Aung San Suu Kyi's, and stating his home address in the caption, inviting arrest. Arrested by soldiers and police that night; held at North Dagon Police Station, then Insein. Charged under Penal Code s.505(a); the junta's statement cited incitement to disrupt peace and stability and spreading propaganda. Sentenced to 20 years on 23 August 2023 - reported as the harshest celebrity sentence of the crackdown.
disputes.response: Byu Har made no public response after arrest. The junta's framing is the response on record.
disputes.evidence: Documented sequence, from independent sources: calls for his arrest circulated on pro-military Telegram channels on 23 May; the channel Ka Ka Han (created Oct 2022) described him as 'a low-class dog who swears because there is a blackout in Yangon'; arrest photos were posted to junta Telegram channels on 24 May.
disputes.corroboration: STRONG - five or more independent outlets: AP, BBC, RFA, Mizzima, The Irrawaddy, Bangkok Post, VOA, PEN America, plus Rappler's investigation of the doxing infrastructure. Rappler documents 32 arrests in Jan-May 2023 from Ka Ka Han posts alone, and a FOEIM school data leak exposing hundreds of students' details.
disputes.corroboratingDetail: CORRECTION: the archive's earlier note dated the Rappler investigation to March 2025. It is 22 August 2023, and the arrest was May 2023. The doxing posts are dated the same day as the video, not as a preceding campaign. AP quotes a family member and says it was unclear which charge he was convicted of, so no single offence is asserted here.
disputes.safety: SEVERE. Living prisoner, 20-year sentence. Do not publish his home address, family details, or the specific Telegram channel handles - the doxing mechanism is the documented cause of the arrest. UN Special Rapporteurs called out Telegram's moderation failure in Myanmar in March 2023.
disputes.statusNote: settled as to arrest and sentence

disputes.claim: At the Overflow Music Festival, Eastern Yangon Event Park, Thingangyun Township, a group led by Wink (Ye Wint Aung, aka Bala) and bkho bain (Thein Min Htike) performed twelve songs including '5.55566'. During that song they used obscene language causing public alarm and scattered condoms into the audience, with thirteen people on stage. Police arrested participants between 3 and 6 November; sixteen people were charged.
disputes.response: No artist response on record. Authorities said legal action would proceed 'to ensure appropriate punishment'.
disputes.evidence: CHARGE SECTION CONFLICT: the Myanmar Police Force statement (via Positive Angle News, 8 Nov 2025) gives case file (P)213/2025, Thuwunna PS, sections 505-A, 294 and 114. Eleven Media Group (9 Nov 2025) reports '505(b) and 294'. The primary police statement says 505-A, so that is used here. Separately, DVB names a different performer, Yul Nay Lwin, in the same 'condoms on stage' story - the two namings are NOT merged.
disputes.corroboration: Independent Burmese and English-language outlets agree on the facts and diverge only on the section number.
disputes.safety: HIGH. Named individuals under active prosecution.
disputes.statusNote: unresolved - charges open, no verdict found. Note the NDSC granted amnesty to 724 prisoners serving 505-A sentences on 26 Nov 2025; whether these sixteen fall in that cohort is UNVERIFIED.

disputes.claim: On 3 April 2021 the SAC announced warrants under Penal Code s.505(a) for twenty individuals including G Fatt, accused of encouraging participation in the Civil Disobedience Movement, supporting the CRPH, and inciting disturbance. DVB published the list on 4 April 2021.
disputes.response: None recorded in the sources reached.
disputes.evidence: Primary: the SAC announcement, published by DVB. A second SAC/MRTV list of around twenty more names under s.505(a) followed on 2 April.
disputes.corroboration: Primary for the warrant itself.
disputes.corroboratingDetail: SEPARATE AND UNRESOLVED: G Fatt was publicly criticised after appearing at the military-held Thingyan festival in Naypyidaw on 13 April 2023. This rests on a single source, Mizzima's Spring Revolution Daily News, a resistance-linked daily; the live page could not be fetched and there is no independent confirmation that the criticism was directed at G Fatt rather than another festival performer. Recorded as unresolved rather than as fact.
disputes.safety: HIGH. G Fatt was a s.505(a) warrant subject in 2021 and a target of public denunciation in 2023. The April 2023 Thingyan period is a documented high-risk window for the whole scene.
disputes.statusNote: settled as to the warrant

disputes.claim: At a FREE album-promotion concert for his album ဇ in Mandalay, with thousands attending, mostly teenagers, multiple fights broke out. A group of four beat a 19-year-old with a two-foot steel pipe after an incidental elbowing on the dance floor. The victim died of head injuries at Mandalay General Hospital. Four attackers aged 17-20 were arrested on site. Eight police and 30 private security (MMC Security) were on duty. A friend filed under ss.114 and 302. The event was shut down.
disputes.response: Y-Zet's own on-record apology, in a Burmese interview of 29 March 2018: he said he did nothing wrong but a young man died, and that he accepts his share of the responsibility.
disputes.evidence: Coconuts Yangon, 12 June 2017; The Irrawaddy (Burmese), 12 June 2017, reporting the arrests; 7Day News, 13 June 2017 (cited via Wayback).
disputes.corroboration: STRONG - three independent accounts including two Burmese-language outlets.
disputes.corroboratingDetail: IMPORTANT CORRECTION: this is NOT a beef killing and must never be linked causally to the 2011 'Shwee Die' diss. The fight began with accidental physical contact while dancing, six years after the track. Wikipedia places the two facts in adjacent sections with no causal link, and the earlier archive note that juxtaposed them has been corrected.
disputes.safety: Record only the published facts. The victim is not named in any source and should not be identified beyond 'a 19-year-old'.

disputes.claim: Arrested 12 March 2008 at a restaurant in Yangon with five friends. Sentenced 20 November 2008 by the Lanmadaw Township court to five years under SLORC Law 6/88 (illegal organising) plus one year for foreign currency - his lawyer stated the currency total was under 10,000 kyat. Transferred to Kawthaung prison. Amnesty International named him a prisoner of conscience. Released 17 May 2011. Minutes before sentencing he wrote: 'I feel sad, but not because of my imprisonment... I feel sad for the future of our country and people... Have the courage to reject the things you don't like.'
disputes.response: His own statements, quoted above. Post-release he said: 'While I was in prison, I reconsidered some of my past actions and I felt very uneasy... I don't feel that I've used my full capabilities to help the country.' In August 2011 police in Mingala Taungnyunt Township banned him from performing at a show on Hmyawzin Island, which he called 'doubly punishing'.
disputes.evidence: Mizzima, Amnesty International, The Irrawaddy, BBC, moemaka (an interview with Khet Mar), multiple.
disputes.corroboration: very strong
disputes.corroboratingDetail: Continued repression after release is part of the record, and matters: a state that releases a dissident and then bans him from performing is a different situation from one that imprisons him.
disputes.safety: Deceased by state execution 25 July 2022. Widow and surviving Acid members are at risk and Acid is under surveillance. Do not name safe houses, family, or current members' locations.
disputes.statusNote: settled as to imprisonment and release

disputes.claim: Rearrested November 2021, charged under the Counterterrorism Law and the Public Property Protection Act, sentenced to death January 2022, and executed 23 July 2022 with Ko Jimmy (Kyaw Min Yu) and two others. The Daily Beast reported, citing four anonymous sources with knowledge of the Yangan underground, that he was top commander of the armed resistance in Yangon.
disputes.response: The resistance movement never publicly acknowledged the claim.
disputes.evidence: The arrest, charge, sentence and execution are documented by NYT, AP, BBC, Mizzima, The Irrawaddy, DVB and others. The resistance-role claim rests on four anonymous sources and has never been publicly confirmed by the movement.
disputes.corroboration: very strong for the execution; the resistance role is anonymous-sourced and unconfirmed.
disputes.corroboratingDetail: Recorded because it is exactly the kind of claim an archive should carry WITH its uncertainty attached. Anonymous sourcing from a conflict zone is not the same as a refuted claim, and it is not the same as a verified one either.
disputes.safety: MAXIMUM. Deceased by state execution. Do not name safe houses or family. Note the Observer's evidence that Telenor data located his safe house.
disputes.statusNote: execution settled; resistance role unresolved and contested in character

disputes.claim: DICKCOUNCIL producer Ko Aye Win, a former B-boy who used to battle frequently, told Insight Myanmar: 'Before the coup I was a B-Boy, I liked to battle a lot. But not anymore... Hip hop rap battles, they always like to provoke each other and talk to each other. So I thought, how about we switch the arrow direction in Dickcouncil, to take on the military junta and Min Aung Hlaing or whoever, like every tyrant across the globe!' The interview host frames it as repurposing an adversarial battle form against a target not accustomed to being spoken to that way. DICKCOUNCIL is described as achieving an unprecedented dynamic of Burmese youth openly dissing Min Aung Hlaing.
disputes.response: The junta's response is the broader crackdown, documented elsewhere in this archive.
disputes.evidence: Extended interview with Ko Aye Win by Shwe Lan Ga Lay, Insight Myanmar, 26 December 2021, published on the blog and as a podcast episode.
disputes.corroboration: STRONG - a named, on-record producer explaining the intent in his own words.
disputes.corroboratingDetail: THE CLEANEST BEEF ANALOGUE IN THE ARCHIVE. Almost every other 'beef' here is a genre label, a veiled personal diss, or a censorship record. This one is a dispute in battle form, aimed at the state, with a named participant explaining the pivot on the record. It is also the pivot point of the whole dataset: the target of the adversarial form migrated from other rappers to the regime.
disputes.safety: Do not characterise any platform as safe. Telegram carried the music and was also the doxing channel that led to arrests.
disputes.targetDescription: the Myanmar military government and Min Aung Hlaing
disputes.statusNote: settled as a statement of intent

disputes.claim: SAC Law No. 48/2025, the Law on the Prevention of Obstruction, Disruption and Sabotage of Multiparty Democratic General Election, was enacted 29 July 2025 with penalties from three years to the death penalty. From 27 October 2025 artists, actors, comedians and directors were arrested for supporting social-media criticism of the state election-awareness film 'Khit Thamine Ko Done Saing Myi Thu Myar'. Khit Thit Media and other outlets were charged as organisations.
disputes.response: The state framing, per Global New Light of Myanmar.
disputes.evidence: GNLM, the law text and the arrest notices; Myanmar Internet Project's running tally; Reuters.
disputes.corroboration: STRONG, but the totals diverge by counting method: Myanmar Internet Project documented 32 named individuals by 14 Nov 2025; the junta claimed 88 charged by 29 Oct 2025; Reuters reported at least 229 by Dec 2025.
disputes.corroboratingDetail: Mostly film and comedy rather than hip-hop, but it is the same s.505-A plus election-law architecture that catches rappers, and it establishes that by 2025 the legal environment had widened well beyond performance. No artist with a record in this dataset has been charged under it.
disputes.safety: high. No hip-hop artist in this dataset is named as charged.
disputes.statusNote: settled as to the arrests; totals unresolved

disputes.claim: STRUCTURAL, NOT INTERPERSONAL. Thar Si Thaw, a famous singer then head of internal affairs at the Myanmar Music Association, testified to VOA in Burmese on 5 October 2016: 'the existing laws cannot give the necessary protection'. He said he was waiting for the government to fulfil its promise to draft a new copyright law and had been writing and revising the draft himself. He cited enforcement against film and song piracy as the immediate crisis, the music industry resisting, and s.32(a)/(c) as the tools police use. A ministry editorial adviser, Maung Shey, said the ministry was 'personally writing' the law. Separately, the state's cultural quarantine created the 'copy thachin' (copy song) genre - foreign hits rewritten into Burmese - with Lay Phyu's Metallica rewrite of 'Enter Sandman' known domestically as 'Exits'.
disputes.response: The state, via the ministry, was drafting a law as of 2016. Whether it was enacted is UNVERIFIED.
disputes.evidence: VOA Burmese, 5 Oct 2016; The World/PRX on copy-track culture; NBC News/AP; The Independent; de Bakker; J.M. Ferguson in Asia Pacific Journal of Anthropology.
disputes.corroboration: STRONG
disputes.corroboratingDetail: THE MOST IMPORTANT FRAME IN THE ARCHIVE. In this scene a credit dispute is usually not a quarrel between artists but an absent legal category. Phyo Layy writes invisibly as a lyricist for Sandi Myint Lwin, Wine Su Khaing Thein and Warso Moe Oo with no public credit and no documented grievance. A specific investigation of credit disputes involving 99 Symphony's INTERNATION and Phyo Layy found NO dispute exists: Phyo Layy does not appear in that album's writer credits at all. Recorded here so the null result is documented rather than mistaken for an oversight.
disputes.safety: low
disputes.targetDescription: the Myanmar state and the Myanmar Music Association

disputes.target: the Myanmar Music Association and the police
disputes.claim: At a hip-hop concert, G-Tone removed his shirt mid-performance to reveal a tattoo. Police officials handcuffed him as soon as he left the stage - reportedly having been persuaded by other musicians to let him finish his set. He was NOT taken into custody, but the police action 'provoked an angry reaction from the crowd'; police then beat audience members, escalating the incident into a riot. Hip-hop star Yatha intervened and was warned not to get involved again. The Myanmar Music Association banned G-Tone, Thuta and Pyi Tha from performing for one year.
disputes.response: None recorded. G-Tone remains active; he appears on the MHA 'Knockout' posse cut of March 2025.
disputes.corroboration: Single-source (DVB) for the incident. The Independent (2013) and de Bakker independently confirm that Myanmar rappers were targeted over tattoos, but with a DIFFERENT description: de Bakker, quoting Yan Yan Chan, describes 'a bald guy wearing Christian rosary beads on his wrist, but he looked sort of like a monk'. The two accounts of the tattoo do not match.
disputes.safety: low (historical). G-Tone is alive and active.

ah-boy.name: Ah Boy
ah-boy.note: Born Kyaw Phyo Tun on 13 Jan 1986 in Myeik, Tanintharyi Division, to a Sino-Mon family; family moved to Yangon when he was 3. Lead vocalist of Rock$tar from 2002, and Wikipedia calls him a 'pioneer of the third generation of Burmese hip hop' - which implies a fourth generation is a recognised category. Solo debut album Ta Yoke Tan (Chinatown) 2007. 'A Ngweh A That Myar' (with ChanMyae MgCho) hit #1 on the JOOX top 100 in 2020 and won the JOOX 2020 Popular Song Award. MEMBERSHIP: lead vocalist of VIP (Rock$tar) from its 2007 formation, and a former member. His exit is the group's documented event; a Feb 2013 Burmese headline implies a grievance about him not fulfilling his role rather than a rupture. Wikipedia calls him a 'pioneer of the third generation of Burmese hip hop', which implies a fourth is a recognised category.

yzet.name: Y-Zet
yzet.note: Long-running Wildboy member and Oasix's duet partner. Born 28 May 1989 in Pyin Oo Lwin, Mandalay REGION - not Mandalay city; school BEHS No. 4 Pyin Oo Lwin, chemistry at Yadanabon University, dropped out 2008. Joined Wildboy 2011. disputes.claim: At a FREE album-promotion concert for his album ဇ in Mandalay, with thousands attending, mostly teenagers, multiple fights broke out. A group of four beat a 19-year-old with a two-foot steel pipe after an incidental elbowing on the dance floor. The victim died of head injuries at Mandalay General Hospital. Four attackers aged 17-20 were arrested on site. Eight police and 30 private security (MMC Security) were on duty. A friend filed under ss.114 and 302. The event was shut down.
disputes.response: Y-Zet's own on-record apology, in a Burmese interview of 29 March 2018: he said he did nothing wrong but a young man died, and that he accepts his share of the responsibility.
disputes.corroboration: STRONG - three independent accounts including two Burmese-language outlets.
disputes.safety: Record only the published facts. The victim is not named in any source and should not be identified beyond 'a 19-year-old'.

disputes.claim: Bobby Soxer (Htet Htet Aung, b. 22 May 1993) and Hlwan Paing were in a relationship from 2009. She declared on Facebook at the end of 2022 that it had ended, stating the cause was Hlwan Paing's involvement with an actress. Wikipedia summarises this as having 'sparked intense online backlash, prompting Hlwan Paing to later admit to the affair'. She responded with the song 'Amyi Tat Pe Pyaw Paing Kwint Mashi' (နာမည်တပ်ပြီးပြောပိုင့်ခွင့်မရှိ - 'No Right to Speak Without Naming Names'), which indirectly blamed the actress.
disputes.response: Hlwan Paing is reported to have admitted the affair. The actress has no recorded response. Note the song's own title is a claim of indirectness - she denied naming names, so reading it as a direct diss is inference.
disputes.corroboration: Wikipedia plus one Burmese outlet. The affair admission is SINGLE-SOURCED and not independently verified. The widely syndicated biography pages all appear to derive from Wikipedia rather than independent reporting.
disputes.safety: The third party is a living person who is NOT named in the song and must not be named here. Do not extend allegations to her.
